items.summary: 📌 TL;DR Three months ago, I decided to start writing consistently on DEV. Twenty-five articles later, I've learned far more than how to write better. I've learned that writing is much more enjoyable when you stop chasing numbers, that some of the best conversations begin in the comments, and that finding your voice takes time. More than anything, I've learned that the topics you're most connected to often become the ones only you can write. If you're new to DEV, or if you're simply curious about my journey, consider this an open Ask Me Anything. Whether you have questions about writing, finding ideas, building a series, engaging with the community, overcoming challenges, or anything else related to your own journey on DEV, I'd be happy to chat. I definitely don't have all the answers, but if anything I've learned over the past three months can help you in any way, I'd love to share what I know. So feel free to ask me anything in the comments. Table of Contents Why I Wanted to Write This From Silent Reader to Writer Lesson 1: Write Because You Enjoy It Lesson 2: Comment More Than You Think You Should Lesson 3: Don't Let Numbers Define Your Journey Lesson 4: Your Voice Will Change Lesson 5: Write What You Can Relate To Lesson 6: Community Makes Ideas Better Lesson 7: It's Okay to Take a Break Final Thoughts Ask Me Anything 💙 🤝 Let's Stay Connected Why I Wanted to Write This When I sat down to write this article, I realized it had been almost three months since I started writing consistently on DEV. During that time, I've published 25 articles, and this one makes 26. It's honestly hard to believe how much has happened in such a short time. I was fortunate enough to have two articles featured in the Top 7, start a series called Dev Opportunity Radar, and eventually launch a website for it. Those are milestones I'm incredibly grateful for, but when I think about these past three months, they aren't the first things that come to mind. What I remember most are the people. The conversations in the comments, the encouragement when I doubted myself, the community members who shared opportunities that became part of Dev Opportunity Radar, and the readers who reached out to tell me an article helped them or introduced them to something they might have otherwise missed. Those moments have meant more to me than any number ever could. I don't consider myself an expert. Three months is only a small part of what I hope will be a much longer journey. But these past few months have taught me lessons I wish someone had shared with me when I first started writing. I hope they help someone who's just beginning their own. From Silent Reader to Writer When I first joined DEV, I spent much more time reading than writing. I'd browse articles, learn from discussions, and admire the people who confidently shared their experiences and ideas. At the same time, I wasn't sure if I had anything meaningful to contribute myself, so for a long time I stayed a quiet reader. I don't think there's anything wrong with that. Every community has people who learn by listening before they feel ready to join the conversation, and I was definitely one of them. Eventually, though, I started leaving comments. Then I shared a few thoughts of my own. Little by little, writing didn't feel quite as intimidating anymore. English isn't my first language, and even today I still reread my articles wondering if I've explained something clearly enough or whether I've made a mistake. That self-doubt hasn't completely disappeared, and honestly, I don't know if it ever will. What's changed is that I've become a little more comfortable pressing Publish anyway, trusting that every article is another chance to learn and improve. If I'd waited until I felt completely confident, I probably would have never written that first article at all. Lesson 1: Write Because You Enjoy It If there's one lesson that stands out above all the others, it's this: write because you genuinely enjoy writing. When I first started, my mood on a given day often depended on how an article was doing. I'd refresh and check my views, reactions, and comments more than I probably should have. I think that's completely normal, especially when you're putting something you've worked hard on out into the world. We all hope people will read it and connect with it. Over time, though, my perspective started to change. I realized that if I only felt happy when an article performed well, I was giving too much control over my enjoyment to something I couldn't control. Views are wonderful. Reactions are wonderful. Being featured is wonderful. I'm incredibly grateful for every single one of those things, but they've become a bonus rather than the reason I write. Today, when an idea pops into my head, the first question I ask myself isn't, "Will this get a lot of views?" It's, "Is this something I'm excited to write about?" If the answer is yes, I usually end up enjoying the entire process, from researching and writing to reading the conversations that follow. The articles I'm proudest of aren't always the ones that reached the most people. They're the ones I enjoyed creating, because those are the ones that feel the most like me. Lesson 2: Comment More Than You Think You Should If I could only give one piece of advice to someone who's new to DEV, it would be this: don't just write. Read. Comment. Join the conversation. When I first started becoming more active here, I thought publishing articles would be the biggest part of my journey. Looking back, I don't think that was true. Some of my favorite memories didn't begin when I clicked Publish. They began in the comments. Over the past three months, I've discovered incredible writers through comment sections, had conversations that made me think differently, and met people I never would have known otherwise. Some of those conversations even inspired future articles, while others introduced me to opportunities, ideas, and perspectives I probably wouldn't have found on my own. Commenting has also changed the way I read. Instead of quickly scrolling to the next article, I spend more time thinking about what the author is trying to say. If something resonates with me, I try to tell them why. If I learn something new, I let them know. Sometimes it's a simple thank you, and other times it turns into a conversation that continues long after the article itself. It's easy to think of DEV as a place where people publish articles, but to me it's much more than that. It's a community where people encourage one another, share ideas, celebrate wins, and learn together. If you're just getting started, don't worry about writing the perfect article on day one. Start by reading what others are sharing. Leave thoughtful comments. Ask questions. Celebrate someone's achievement. Share your perspective when you have something to add. You never know where a single conversation might lead. Writing brought me to DEV, but the conversations are what made me feel like I belonged here. Lesson 3: Don't Let Numbers Define Your Journey Every notification used to feel exciting, and honestly, every time an article didn't perform the way I'd hoped, it was hard not to wonder what I could have done differently. Looking back, I was checking my stats way more than they deserved. I think that's something many of us experience when we start sharing our work publicly. Over time, though, I realized I was comparing my beginning to someone else's journey. Some writers have been part of the community for years. Some have built an audience over a long period of time. Others have found a niche they're known for. It's not really a fair comparison because everyone's path looks different. I also realized that numbers don't tell the whole story. An article with fewer views might spark an amazing discussion. A single comment from someone saying your article helped them can mean more than hundreds of extra reactions. Some of my favorite articles haven't necessarily been my most popular ones, and that's completely okay. These days, I still look at my article stats because I think it's natural to be curious, but they no longer decide whether I consider an article a success. What matters more is whether I enjoyed writing it, whether I learned something through the process, and whether it started a meaningful conversation. One example of this for me is Dev Opportunity Radar. When I first started the series, I'll admit I hoped it would reach more people than it has so far. There are weeks where I wish it had more views because I believe these opportunities could help more developers. Maybe there are things I can improve, and I'm always trying to learn. But I've realized something more important: I can't let those numbers decide whether I keep showing up every Friday. I started Dev Opportunity Radar because I kept discovering amazing fellowships, grants, hackathons, and resources after it was already too late to apply. I didn't want other people to miss those opportunities for the same reason. That purpose hasn't changed just because a particular edition gets fewer views than I hoped. What's interesting is that the numbers only tell part of the story. If you only looked at the view count, you might think the series isn't doing particularly well. But when I read the comments, it's a completely different picture. People share opportunities I would have never found on my own. They celebrate getting accepted into programs. They suggest improvements, contribute Community Finds, and tell me an edition helped them discover something they would have otherwise missed. That reminds me that impact isn't always measured by views or reactions. Sometimes it's measured by the conversations you start and the people you help, even when those numbers aren't immediately visible. Dev Opportunity Radar has changed me more than I expected. It gave me a reason to show up every Friday and helped me find a place in the community that feels uniquely my own. Even if only a handful of people read each edition, that's still a handful of people I have the chance to help, and to me, that's reason enough to keep going. Lesson 4: Your Voice Will Change One of the biggest misconceptions I had when I started writing was that I needed to figure out my writing style before I could become a consistent writer. I don't think that's how it works at all. I think you discover your voice by writing. Every article teaches you something new about how you think, what you enjoy writing about, and how you connect with readers. As you keep writing, your confidence grows, your ideas become clearer, and you slowly begin to understand what feels authentic to you. When I look back at some of my earlier articles, I can already see changes in the way I write. Some things I'd explain differently today, and there are ideas I'd probably approach from a different angle. I don't see that as a bad thing. If anything, it's a sign that I'm learning. Even today, I don't think I've found my final writing voice, and honestly, I hope I never fully do. I hope it continues to evolve as I learn new things, meet new people, and gain new experiences. To me, that's one of the most exciting parts of writing. Every article becomes another small step in that journey. So if you're just starting out, don't put too much pressure on yourself to find your "voice" before you begin. Start writing, keep showing up, and give yourself permission to grow. You might be surprised by how much your writing changes a few months from now. Lesson 5: Write What You Can Relate To The articles I've enjoyed writing the most all have one thing in common. They came from experiences I could genuinely relate to. Dev Opportunity Radar is the clearest example. As I mentioned earlier, it grew out of a frustration I'd lived through myself: missing opportunities simply because I found out about them too late. The opportunity itself was rarely the problem. Access to information was. That experience made me wonder how many other people were missing opportunities for the exact same reason. So I decided to start sharing the fellowships, grants, hackathons, and resources I came across each week, hoping someone else would discover them while there was still time to apply. It taught me something I keep coming back to. The articles people connect with the most aren't always about the most popular topics. They're often the ones that come from experiences only you have lived, because those experiences give you a perspective nobody else can write in quite the same way. If I could give one more piece of advice, it would be this: don't spend too much time trying to figure out what everyone else wants you to write. Instead, think about the experiences you've had, the challenges you've faced, the things you've learned, or even the problems you've wished someone had solved for you. Sometimes the best ideas come from asking yourself, "What do I wish I had known a year ago?" That's still the reason I enjoy putting Dev Opportunity Radar together every Friday. The purpose has always been bigger than the numbers. Lesson 6: Community Makes Ideas Better One of the biggest surprises over the past three months is realizing that writing isn't really a solo activity. Every article may begin with one person behind a keyboard, but it rarely ends there. Every time I press Publish, the article becomes something more because of the people who take the time to read it. Their comments make me think differently. Their questions inspire future articles. Sometimes they share their own experiences, and I end up learning just as much from them as they do from me. That's one of my favorite parts of writing on DEV: every article becomes the beginning of a conversation rather than the end of one. Dev Opportunity Radar is probably the best example of this. I may be the one putting each edition together, but the series has never really felt like something I build alone. Community Finds was there from the very first edition because I wanted it to be a space where everyone could share opportunities, not just me. Since then, people have continued contributing opportunities I would've otherwise missed, Reader Updates have given people a chance to celebrate their own milestones, and the series has even grown into its own website. It no longer feels like just my series. It's become something the community helps build every week, and much bigger than I could have built on my own. Being part of that has changed me in ways I never expected. It's introduced me to incredible people and given me a place in this community that feels uniquely my own. More than anything else, these past three months have reminded me that communities grow because people choose to contribute in their own way. Some write articles. Some leave thoughtful comments. Some answer questions, share opportunities, or simply encourage someone who's just getting started. Every one of those contributions matters, and together they create the kind of community people want to come back to. A few people deserve a special mention here. @webdeveloperhyper , @klaudiagrz , @francistrdev , @javz , @technogamerz , @xulingfeng , @csm18 , @itsugo and @shubhradev , thank you for always supporting me. On so many of my posts, you show up with a reaction or a comment, and it means a lot every single time. You've become friends at this point, and I always look forward to seeing you around the community. I know I won't be able to name everyone who's supported me, and there are honestly so many more people who've been part of this in ways big and small. If I've missed your name, please don't take it personally. It's not intentional, and I'm just as grateful to you as to anyone I've named. And to everyone else who's followed along and kept supporting my work, thank you. Whether you follow me here on DEV, read one article or all 25, left a comment, hit react, or simply read quietly without saying a word, that support means just as much to me. A reaction on a day I wasn't sure about an article has meant just as much as a comment or a message. You've helped shape my experience on DEV far more than you probably realize. Lesson 7: It's Okay to Take a Break One thing I've learned over the past three months is that it's okay to take a step back every now and then. Last week was actually the first week in a while where I didn't publish a new article, apart from Dev Opportunity Radar. It wasn't because I had run out of ideas or because I didn't want to write. I simply didn't have a topic that I genuinely felt excited about, and I didn't want to force one just for the sake of staying consistent. If you're just getting started, I do think it helps to have a gentle goal. Maybe that's one article a week or even one every couple of weeks. Having a small target can help you build a routine without making writing feel like another obligation. That said, I don't think every goal has to be followed perfectly. I usually aim to publish one article a week (apart from Dev Opportunity Radar), but if I don't have an idea that genuinely excites me, I'd rather wait than force something just to stay on schedule. In my experience, the more you write, read, and interact with the community, the more ideas naturally start to appear. I think there's a lot of pressure online to always be creating, always publishing, and always staying visible. For me, writing has always been something I look forward to, and I'd like to keep it that way. At the end of the day, we're all human. The hobbies, passions, and projects we care about shouldn't become another source of burnout. If taking a short break means coming back with more excitement and fresh ideas, that's a much healthier approach than forcing yourself to create something your heart isn't really in. Final Thoughts Three months ago, I simply wanted to become a better writer. I realize now I gained much more than that. I became a little more confident every time I pressed Publish, discovered topics I genuinely enjoy writing about, found a community that constantly inspires me, and watched a small idea born from one of my own frustrations grow into something much bigger than I ever imagined. If there's one thing these past three months have taught me, it's that writing is about so much more than publishing articles. It's about sharing experiences, learning from one another, and becoming part of a community where people genuinely want to see each other succeed. Some of the best parts of this journey didn't begin when I clicked Publish. They began when someone replied, shared their perspective, or simply started a conversation. I don't know what the next three months will look like, and I hope they surprise me just as much as the last three have. I'm sure my writing will continue to evolve, my interests will change, and hopefully I'll keep finding new ways to contribute to this amazing community. For now, I'm simply grateful that I decided to press Publish on that first article. Ask Me Anything 💙 If you've made it this far, thank you so much for reading. Writing these articles has taught me a lot, but one of my favorite parts has always been the conversations that happen after I press Publish, so it felt fitting to end this reflection with a conversation too. Everything I've shared here simply comes from my own experiences over the past few months, and I'm sure there's plenty I still have to learn. So if you're new to DEV, thinking about writing your first article, curious about Dev Opportunity Radar, or even feeling a little nervous about pressing Publish for the first time, feel free to ask me anything. Writing, finding ideas, building a series, engaging with the community, or anything else on your mind. If I know the answer, I'll share it. If I don't, I'll be honest about that too. I'd also love to hear about your own journey. A lesson you've learned, a tip that's helped you, or something you're excited or nervous about if you're just starting out. My hope is that the comments become more than a Q&A between you and me, a place where everyone shares stories and lessons that might help someone else just beginning their own. I'm looking forward to chatting with all of you down there 💙 🤝 Let's Stay Connected Place Find me here GitHub building things → hemapriya-kanagala LinkedIn resources & updates → hemapriya-kanagala X random dev thoughts → @KanagalaHema Transparency note: The banner image for this article was generated using DEV Community's built-in AI image generation feature. I wrote the prompt, generated multiple variations, and selected the final image used in this post.

That experience made me wonder how many other people were missing opportunities for the exact same reason. So I decided to start sharing the fellowships, grants, hackathons, and resources I came across each week, hoping someone else would discover them while there was still time to apply.

It taught me something I keep coming back to. The articles people connect with the most aren't always about the most popular topics. They're often the ones that come from experiences only you have lived, because those experiences give you a perspective nobody else can write in quite the same way.

If I could give one more piece of advice, it would be this: don't spend too much time trying to figure out what everyone else wants you to write. Instead, think about the experiences you've had, the challenges you've faced, the things you've learned, or even the problems you've wished someone had solved for you. Sometimes the best ideas come from asking yourself, "What do I wish I had known a year ago?"

That's still the reason I enjoy putting Dev Opportunity Radar together every Friday. The purpose has always been bigger than the numbers.

Lesson 6: Community Makes Ideas Better

One of the biggest surprises over the past three months is realizing that writing isn't really a solo activity. Every article may begin with one person behind a keyboard, but it rarely ends there.

Every time I press Publish, the article becomes something more because of the people who take the time to read it. Their comments make me think differently. Their questions inspire future articles. Sometimes they share their own experiences, and I end up learning just as much from them as they do from me. That's one of my favorite parts of writing on DEV: every article becomes the beginning of a conversation rather than the end of one.

Dev Opportunity Radar is probably the best example of this. I may be the one putting each edition together, but the series has never really felt like something I build alone. Community Finds was there from the very first edition because I wanted it to be a space where everyone could share opportunities, not just me. Since then, people have continued contributing opportunities I would've otherwise missed, Reader Updates have given people a chance to celebrate their own milestones, and the series has even grown into its own website. It no longer feels like just my series.

It's become something the community helps build every week, and much bigger than I could have built on my own.

Being part of that has changed me in ways I never expected. It's introduced me to incredible people and given me a place in this community that feels uniquely my own.

More than anything else, these past three months have reminded me that communities grow because people choose to contribute in their own way. Some write articles. Some leave thoughtful comments. Some answer questions, share opportunities, or simply encourage someone who's just getting started. Every one of those contributions matters, and together they create the kind of community people want to come back to.

A few people deserve a special mention here. @webdeveloperhyper, @klaudiagrz, @francistrdev, @javz, @technogamerz, @xulingfeng, @csm18, @itsugo and @shubhradev, thank you for always supporting me. On so many of my posts, you show up with a reaction or a comment, and it means a lot every single time. You've become friends at this point, and I always look forward to seeing you around the community.

I know I won't be able to name everyone who's supported me, and there are honestly so many more people who've been part of this in ways big and small. If I've missed your name, please don't take it personally. It's not intentional, and I'm just as grateful to you as to anyone I've named.

And to everyone else who's followed along and kept supporting my work, thank you. Whether you follow me here on DEV, read one article or all 25, left a comment, hit react, or simply read quietly without saying a word, that support means just as much to me. A reaction on a day I wasn't sure about an article has meant just as much as a comment or a message. You've helped shape my experience on DEV far more than you probably realize.

Lesson 7: It's Okay to Take a Break

One thing I've learned over the past three months is that it's okay to take a step back every now and then.

Last week was actually the first week in a while where I didn't publish a new article, apart from Dev Opportunity Radar. It wasn't because I had run out of ideas or because I didn't want to write.

I simply didn't have a topic that I genuinely felt excited about, and I didn't want to force one just for the sake of staying consistent.

If you're just getting started, I do think it helps to have a gentle goal. Maybe that's one article a week or even one every couple of weeks. Having a small target can help you build a routine without making writing feel like another obligation.

That said, I don't think every goal has to be followed perfectly. I usually aim to publish one article a week (apart from Dev Opportunity Radar), but if I don't have an idea that genuinely excites me, I'd rather wait than force something just to stay on schedule. In my experience, the more you write, read, and interact with the community, the more ideas naturally start to appear.

I think there's a lot of pressure online to always be creating, always publishing, and always staying visible. For me, writing has always been something I look forward to, and I'd like to keep it that way.

At the end of the day, we're all human. The hobbies, passions, and projects we care about shouldn't become another source of burnout. If taking a short break means coming back with more excitement and fresh ideas, that's a much healthier approach than forcing yourself to create something your heart isn't really in.

Final Thoughts

Three months ago, I simply wanted to become a better writer. I realize now I gained much more than that.

I became a little more confident every time I pressed Publish, discovered topics I genuinely enjoy writing about, found a community that constantly inspires me, and watched a small idea born from one of my own frustrations grow into something much bigger than I ever imagined.

If there's one thing these past three months have taught me, it's that writing is about so much more than publishing articles. It's about sharing experiences, learning from one another, and becoming part of a community where people genuinely want to see each other succeed. Some of the best parts of this journey didn't begin when I clicked Publish. They began when someone replied, shared their perspective, or simply started a conversation.

I don't know what the next three months will look like, and I hope they surprise me just as much as the last three have. I'm sure my writing will continue to evolve, my interests will change, and hopefully I'll keep finding new ways to contribute to this amazing community.

For now, I'm simply grateful that I decided to press Publish on that first article.

Ask Me Anything 💙

If you've made it this far, thank you so much for reading. Writing these articles has taught me a lot, but one of my favorite parts has always been the conversations that happen after I press Publish, so it felt fitting to end this reflection with a conversation too.

Everything I've shared here simply comes from my own experiences over the past few months, and I'm sure there's plenty I still have to learn. So if you're new to DEV, thinking about writing your first article, curious about Dev Opportunity Radar, or even feeling a little nervous about pressing Publish for the first time, feel free to ask me anything. Writing, finding ideas, building a series, engaging with the community, or anything else on your mind. If I know the answer, I'll share it. If I don't, I'll be honest about that too.

I'd also love to hear about your own journey. A lesson you've learned, a tip that's helped you, or something you're excited or nervous about if you're just starting out.

My hope is that the comments become more than a Q&A between you and me, a place where everyone shares stories and lessons that might help someone else just beginning their own.

I'm looking forward to chatting with all of you down there 💙

🤝 Let's Stay Connected

items.title: Sir Shortoken: Bullet Mode, Local Expansion, and What Actually Held Up
items.summary: TL;DR: Tested whether representing Claude's responses as bullets instead of prose loses any information. Ran it across 14 technical topics — 24-78% token savings depending on compression level, fidelity held up on 12 of 14 runs, and 2 runs (same topic, three attempts) had the local expansion model fabricate a detail. Built a Chrome extension that expands bullets back into prose locally via Ollama, so the frontier model only pays for reasoning. GitHub: https://github.com/shouvik12/sir-shortoken Background Sir Shortoken is a system prompt that constrains Claude/GPT/Gemini to answer within information budgets — Quick, Balanced, Deep, Unlimited — instead of defaulting to maximum elaboration on every question. The natural follow-up question once that was working: prose isn't the only way to represent a constrained answer. What if the response was bullets instead — stripped of connective language, just the structural content? Would that hold up, or would compressing the format also compress out information that mattered? The hypothesis Bullets and prose aren't necessarily lossy relative to each other — they're two different representations of the same underlying content. Prose adds transitions, connective phrasing, and narrative flow. Bullets drop that scaffolding and keep the structure. If that's true, there's an interesting architecture hiding in it: the expensive model (Claude) only has to pay tokens for the reasoning — getting the facts and structure right. The rendering — turning that structure into readable prose — doesn't need frontier-level intelligence. A much smaller local model should be able to do that part for close to free. The extension Built a small Chrome extension that sits on Claude.ai. When Sir Shortoken responds in bullets, an "Expand to Prose" button appears under that message. Clicking it sends the bullet content to a local model — I used qwen2.5:7b through Ollama, running entirely on-machine, no API calls — which rewrites the bullets into normal prose in roughly 10-15 seconds. The button is attached to that specific message in the DOM, not to the current view. Scroll away, come back to an earlier message in a long conversation, the button is still there and still expands that same response. You're not committed to reading an entire conversation in bullets just because one message used that format. Two implementation details worth calling out for anyone trying to reproduce this: CORS: Ollama needs to be started with OLLAMA_ORIGINS="chrome-extension://*" ollama serve or the extension gets a 403 on every request. Extraction: The content script has to be careful about what text it sends to the local model. Early versions grabbed the entire message DOM node's innerText, which included Claude's reasoning-summary line and the Sir Shortoken Ledger block — both ended up getting narrated into the expanded prose ("Claude responded with 'OAuth 2.'...") instead of just expanding the actual bullet content. Fixed by stripping everything from Sir Shortoken's Ledger onward and everything before the first real bullet line. The 14-run test Ran the same pipeline — bullets out of Sir Shortoken, then expansion via the local model — across 14 different technical topics, at two compression levels (Standard and Aggressive). Measured token counts at each stage and read every expansion manually to check whether anything was dropped or invented. Topic   Compression Prose   Bullets Savings Fidelity StatefulSet Standard    363 277 24% Clean Git merge/rebase    Standard    715 215 70% Clean Rate limiting   Standard    363 120 67% Clean CSS specificity Standard    246 148 40% Clean JWT auth    Standard    349 202 42% Clean ACID transactions   Standard    519 251 52% Clean Load balancing  Standard    602 374 38% Minor drop DNS resolution  Aggressive  463 104 78% Clean Raft leader election    Aggressive  502 122 76% Clean TCP handshake   Standard    233 108 54% Minor drop HTTP/2 mux (1st)    Aggressive  323 74  77% Fabrication Virtual memory/paging   Aggressive  594 179 70% Clean HTTP/2 mux (2nd)    Aggressive  324 91  72% Clean HTTP/2 mux (3rd)    Aggressive  324 91  72% Fabrication Savings: ranged 24-78% depending on compression mode. Standard compression averaged roughly 48%; Aggressive averaged closer to 75%. Fidelity: 10 of 14 runs expanded cleanly, with no facts dropped and nothing invented. 2 runs (load balancing, TCP handshake) had minor drops — a term omitted here or there, nothing structurally wrong. 2 runs fabricated a detail that wasn't present in the source bullets. The fabrication finding Both fabrication cases were the same topic — HTTP/2 multiplexing — run as three separate attempts. It failed on the 1st and 3rd attempts, and expanded clean on the 2nd. That's not evenly distributed across the dataset. Every other topic tested, including some fairly dense ones (Raft leader election, virtual memory paging), expanded cleanly every time it was run. HTTP/2 multiplexing failed 2 out of 3 tries on the same content. That pattern — concentrated on one topic rather than spread randomly across the dataset — suggests this isn't just noise you average away. It's more consistent with the local model having weaker or more ambiguous training signal on that specific topic, and filling gaps with something plausible-sounding rather than sticking strictly to what was in the bullets. I don't have a confirmed root cause yet. It could be topic-specific (something about how HTTP/2 internals are represented in the smaller model's training data), or it could be an artifact of how compressed the Aggressive-mode bullets were for that particular topic. Worth noting all four fidelity issues (2 minor, 2 fabrication) occurred in runs using either Standard compression on a dense topic or Aggressive compression generally — none occurred on a "medium density, standard compression" combination, though the sample size is too small to treat that as more than an observation. What this means practically The architecture works: token savings are real, and most content expands faithfully. But "trust the local expansion blindly" isn't a claim the data supports yet. For anything where getting a fact wrong actually matters, treat the expanded prose as a first draft on unfamiliar topics rather than a guaranteed-faithful rendering — especially if the source bullets were generated at Aggressive compression. The 60-78% number is the one that's tempting to lead with, but the more useful finding is that fabrication risk appears to be topic-correlated rather than randomly distributed. That's the thing worth verifying if anyone reproduces this — does it hold up the same way with a different local model, or is qwen2.5:7b specifically weaker on networking-protocol internals? Try it /balanced /bullets Explain OAuth 2.0 Repo, skill.md, and the extension are all up: https://github.com/shouvik12/sir-shortoken Genuinely curious whether anyone else sees the same topic-specific fabrication pattern, or if it's particular to this setup.

items.title: Markdown Studio - a browser-based HTML-to-Markdown converter
items.summary: Hi - I built a small browser-based project called MD Studio: mdstudio.dev It started as a personal project to help me learn AI-assisted web development and Markdown, which I realised was used a lot in AI tools and software-development workflows. MD Studio lets you: Paste rich text or import HTML and convert it to Markdown Edit the converted Markdown Preview the rendered result Switch between GFM and CommonMark profiles Copy, download or print the result It’s built with Preact, TypeScript, CodeMirror and Vite. It runs without an account or installation, and document content is processed locally in the browser. This is a non-commercial learning project. I’d really appreciate feedback on confusing interface choices, conversion problems, browser issues or anything important I may have overlooked. Feedback is welcome in the comments or through the public feedback repository: https://github.com/marc-reid/md-studio-feedback Thanks!

items.title: Kiro and the Future of AI-Assisted Development
items.summary: I started using Kiro at work and am incredibly impressed by how it transforms our AI coding workflow. Instead of writing code first and refactoring later (the typical loop with Copilot and ChatGPT), Kiro uses a spec-driven approach. The Kiro methodology — moving from requirements to technical design to tasks — perfectly solves a challenge I had been trying to fix with GitHub Copilot. I wanted a way to define structured instructions first and then generate the code, but Kiro automates that whole initial planning phase for me. Below are my first impressions of Kiro after a few weeks of hands-on use. If you are currently using GitHub's AI tool, you can also check out my other article for some great ways to supercharge your workflow with Github Copilot . What is Kiro? Kiro is an Integrated Development Environment (IDE) built by AWS on the open-source version of VS Code ( Code OSS ) - so it combines all the VS Code advantages and extensions with a built-in AI tool optimized for spec-driven development. Unlike traditional AI assistants that generate code from chat prompts, Kiro focuses on specifications first. You define the blueprint, turn it into a clear list of tasks, and then decide whether to run them one by one or all at once. Kiro Agents Kiro agents use the same concept as Copilot agents: they are autonomous, specialized AI assistants that you can choose based on the specific task you want help with . Kiro also comes with a few built-in agents that you can select when starting a new chat session, and you can also create your own agents: Spec : Focuses on the planning phase to map out feature requirements, technical design and tasks. Plan : Analyzes the codebase to help you to resolve questions you have and plan how to coordinate the coding workflow. Bug Fix : Debugs your code by catching errors and applying immediate corrections. Note: Depending on the version of Kiro you are using, you may see a slightly different set of agents, but the Spec agent is the one we will focus on in this article. AGENTS.md This file is used by AI tools in every chat interaction, so it is worth setting up properly. To unlock Kiro's full power, create an AGENTS.md file at your project root. It should capture the main system requirements, such as those provided by the architecture team, along with any important tech stack constraints and the essential commands for the project. Keep it concise and avoid over-explaining or redundancy. You can find examples at agents.md . Kiro specs This is where Kiro really shines. The workflow for Kiro specs follows a recommended path: Requirements → Design → Tasks . These files are created before any code changes are made. While you can technically skip ahead and start with Design, Kiro strongly advises beginning with Requirements. Whichever path you choose, Kiro automatically saves these files inside a dedicated feature folder within a hidden .kiro/ directory at your project root. Your browser does not support the video tag. You can also watch the video on Kiro's site . Source: Kiro documentation. The idea here is to create specs grouped by feature. Each feature could correspond to a Jira ticket, for example. This is different from AGENTS.md , which contains the core instructions for the project. In this case, we ask Kiro to focus on the specific parts of the project we are implementing. Let's dive into them below. Requirements.md This is your entry point: Kiro will generate a clear list of user stories and constraints that is easy for anyone to read. To create the spec, make sure the Spec agent is active (you can select it whenever you start a new chat session, as explained above). Then ask Kiro to define the requirements, clearly stating what should and should not be implemented at this stage. For example, you can base the instructions on the Jira ticket requirements. Kiro will ask whether this is a new feature and, if so, group related specs into a new folder within .kiro/ . Keep your instructions narrow and precise. For example, imagine a web app with several features. The AGENTS.md file would hold the core project requirements, while a chat prompt could ask Kiro to create requirements for a new feature, such as: "Create the requirements for a new feature. It should focus on X, but should not include Y." Here, X and Y are short lists of things to include or exclude. Once the initial draft is ready, Kiro will ask whether you want to refine the requirements. If so, it will prompt you with a series of refinement questions to improve the document, or you can ask it to apply the necessary changes directly. Design.md Once the requirements are locked, Kiro asks for permission to move on to the technical design phase. Based on the requirements, it generates technical blueprints tailored to your stack — data models, infrastructure needs, example code snippets, and component diagrams. Concrete examples Kiro can produce: Folder structure and file names it will create (so you can review layout before code is written). TypeScript interfaces or JSON schemas for the data models the feature will use. API contract examples (endpoints, request/response shapes) or OpenAPI fragments. Small, runnable code snippets or migration scripts the agents will apply. As before, review these outputs and make any adjustments before moving on to the implementation tasks. Tasks.md In this final step, Kiro converts your technical design into a dependency-aware checklist of implementation tasks. Tasks are grouped by step so you can follow the implementation flow (see the video above for a demo). Click on a task to apply it and watch progress in the UI: an animated icon shows work in progress and a checkmark appears when the task completes. You can run tasks one-by-one, by group, or all at once. I recommend running them individually or in small groups so you can review changes as they happen and request improvements if needed. Additional Kiro features Kiro includes several other useful features — check the official documentation for full details. Autopilot : gives you control over how the AI applies changes. You can run everything automatically in Autopilot mode, or approve each step manually in Supervised mode. Steering : similar to Copilot, Kiro lets you define rules for specific contexts using frontmatter in Markdown files. For example, you can create custom instructions for TypeScript files only. These instructions can be applied automatically or manually through the chat prompt and can target the repository, workspace, or global level. Slash commands : let you run custom instructions from chat. For example, you could create a steering rule or hook that generates a commit message whenever you type /create-commit-msg , then analyze the diff and suggest a concise message that follows your preferred pattern. Checkpoints : because Kiro creates checkpoints throughout a chat, you can click "Restore" to rewind both your code changes and the Kiro context. It is essentially an undo button. Custom agents : as mentioned before, Kiro comes with some prebuilt agents, but you can also create your own for specific needs, such as a developer agent with tailored instructions. This agent will then be available when you start a new session. Conclusion What I like most about Kiro is that it feels less like a chatbot and more like a thoughtful collaborator. It has helped me structure my work better and stay more intentional about the code I write, especially as I move from refactoring to planning. If you enjoy building with AI in a more guided way, I think it is absolutely worth trying. 😊

You define the blueprint, turn it into a clear list of tasks, and then decide whether to run them one by one or all at once.

Kiro Agents

Kiro agents use the same concept as Copilot agents: they are autonomous, specialized AI assistants that you can choose based on the specific task you want help with. Kiro also comes with a few built-in agents that you can select when starting a new chat session, and you can also create your own agents:

  • Spec: Focuses on the planning phase to map out feature requirements, technical design and tasks.
  • Plan: Analyzes the codebase to help you to resolve questions you have and plan how to coordinate the coding workflow.
  • Bug Fix: Debugs your code by catching errors and applying immediate corrections.

Note: Depending on the version of Kiro you are using, you may see a slightly different set of agents, but the Spec agent is the one we will focus on in this article.

AGENTS.md

This file is used by AI tools in every chat interaction, so it is worth setting up properly. To unlock Kiro's full power, create an AGENTS.md file at your project root. It should capture the main system requirements, such as those provided by the architecture team, along with any important tech stack constraints and the essential commands for the project. Keep it concise and avoid over-explaining or redundancy. You can find examples at agents.md.

Kiro specs

This is where Kiro really shines. The workflow for Kiro specs follows a recommended path: Requirements → Design → Tasks. These files are created before any code changes are made. While you can technically skip ahead and start with Design, Kiro strongly advises beginning with Requirements. Whichever path you choose, Kiro automatically saves these files inside a dedicated feature folder within a hidden .kiro/ directory at your project root.

Your browser does not support the video tag. You can also watch the video on Kiro's site.

Source: Kiro documentation.

The idea here is to create specs grouped by feature. Each feature could correspond to a Jira ticket, for example. This is different from AGENTS.md, which contains the core instructions for the project. In this case, we ask Kiro to focus on the specific parts of the project we are implementing.

Let's dive into them below.

Requirements.md

This is your entry point: Kiro will generate a clear list of user stories and constraints that is easy for anyone to read.

To create the spec, make sure the Spec agent is active (you can select it whenever you start a new chat session, as explained above). Then ask Kiro to define the requirements, clearly stating what should and should not be implemented at this stage. For example, you can base the instructions on the Jira ticket requirements. Kiro will ask whether this is a new feature and, if so, group related specs into a new folder within .kiro/. Keep your instructions narrow and precise.

For example, imagine a web app with several features. The AGENTS.md file would hold the core project requirements, while a chat prompt could ask Kiro to create requirements for a new feature, such as: "Create the requirements for a new feature. It should focus on X, but should not include Y." Here, X and Y are short lists of things to include or exclude.

Once the initial draft is ready, Kiro will ask whether you want to refine the requirements. If so, it will prompt you with a series of refinement questions to improve the document, or you can ask it to apply the necessary changes directly.

Design.md

Once the requirements are locked, Kiro asks for permission to move on to the technical design phase. Based on the requirements, it generates technical blueprints tailored to your stack — data models, infrastructure needs, example code snippets, and component diagrams.

Concrete examples Kiro can produce:

  • Folder structure and file names it will create (so you can review layout before code is written).
  • TypeScript interfaces or JSON schemas for the data models the feature will use.
  • API contract examples (endpoints, request/response shapes) or OpenAPI fragments.
  • Small, runnable code snippets or migration scripts the agents will apply.

As before, review these outputs and make any adjustments before moving on to the implementation tasks.

Tasks.md

In this final step, Kiro converts your technical design into a dependency-aware checklist of implementation tasks. Tasks are grouped by step so you can follow the implementation flow (see the video above for a demo). Click on a task to apply it and watch progress in the UI: an animated icon shows work in progress and a checkmark appears when the task completes.

You can run tasks one-by-one, by group, or all at once. I recommend running them individually or in small groups so you can review changes as they happen and request improvements if needed.

Additional Kiro features

Kiro includes several other useful features — check the official documentation for full details.

  • Autopilot: gives you control over how the AI applies changes. You can run everything automatically in Autopilot mode, or approve each step manually in Supervised mode.

  • Steering: similar to Copilot, Kiro lets you define rules for specific contexts using frontmatter in Markdown files. For example, you can create custom instructions for TypeScript files only. These instructions can be applied automatically or manually through the chat prompt and can target the repository, workspace, or global level.

  • Slash commands: let you run custom instructions from chat. For example, you could create a steering rule or hook that generates a commit message whenever you type /create-commit-msg, then analyze the diff and suggest a concise message that follows your preferred pattern.

  • Checkpoints: because Kiro creates checkpoints throughout a chat, you can click "Restore" to rewind both your code changes and the Kiro context. It is essentially an undo button.

  • Custom agents: as mentioned before, Kiro comes with some prebuilt agents, but you can also create your own for specific needs, such as a developer agent with tailored instructions. This agent will then be available when you start a new session.

Conclusion

What I like most about Kiro is that it feels less like a chatbot and more like a thoughtful collaborator. It has helped me structure my work better and stay more intentional about the code I write, especially as I move from refactoring to planning. If you enjoy building with AI in a more guided way, I think it is absolutely worth trying. 😊

items.title: The cost of running the White House, from staff salaries to subscription services
items.summary: Construction of a new helipad on the South Lawn of the White House continues. Finn Gomez/Getty Images Running the White House Office and Residence costs millions every year. The White House Office is expected to spend about $51 million on permanent staff pay in fiscal 2026. Using government data, Business Insider compiled the costs of running the White House. Keeping the White House running is no small feat — and comes at no small cost. With 132 rooms, 35 bathrooms, and a kitchen capable of serving dinner to as many as 140 guests and hors d'oeuvres to more than 1,000, looking after the residence is a lot of work. Then there's the cost of White House operations, which includes tens of millions of dollars a year in staff compensation and travel. Business Insider compiled a list of costs associated with running the White House using data from the Office of Management and Budget and government spending data. They include a mix of approved funding, money committed to be spent, and full-year estimates. Typically, White House expenses are funded by taxpayers through congressional appropriations. Some costs, such as current renovation work, are listed as reimbursable, meaning that another source will repay the account. Here's a breakdown of some of the costs of running the White House. White House Executive Residence personnel President Donald Trump hosted a Rose Garden Club dinner Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images Butlers, housekeepers, chefs, doormen, florists, and electricians, among other staff, work to keep the White House running, all under the purview of the White House's chief usher. About 90 to 100 staff work at the Executive Residence, according to the White House Historical Association. The Executive Residence reported roughly $9 million in personnel-compensation obligations for fiscal 2025. That included roughly $8 million for permanent full-time staff and $1 million in other employee pay. It also reported about $3 million in employee benefits. OMB estimates the same compensation and benefit costs for fiscal 2026. For fiscal 2027, it proposes about $11 million in compensation and $4 million in benefits. Executive Residence supplies King Charles III and Queen Camilla speak with chef Carlo Figarella as they tour the South Lawn at the White House on day one of their US State Visit. Suzanne Plunkett - Pool via Samir Hussein/WireImage For fiscal 2025, communications, utilities, and miscellaneous charges were roughly $1 million, and another roughly $1 million in supplies and materials. The OMB estimates similar amounts for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same figures for fiscal 2027. White House Office personnel compensation White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt. Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty Images A separate account pays for White House Office staff and operations, including advisors and administrative staff who directly support the president. As of July 1, 2026, there were 411 White House staffers, including 365 employees and 46 full- or part-time detailees, according to the annual report to Congress on White House Office Personnel. Salaries and employee benefits make up most of the White House Office's operating budget. Some of the highest-paid White House staffers include Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, and Director of Speechwriting Ross Worthington, who each earn $195,200, according to a recent personnel report. While nothing to sniff at, these government salaries lag behind what professionals often earn in the private sector. Congress appropriated $78.9 million for White House staff and operations in fiscal 2026, the same amount appropriated for fiscal 2025. For fiscal 2025, the White House Office recorded about $43 million in compensation for permanent full-time staff. OMB estimates that this will rise to about $51 million for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same amount for fiscal 2027. The president's compensation US President Donald Trump at the Oval Office, the main office of the president. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images The salary for the president is fixed at $400,000, plus a $50,000 allowance for official expenses. Before taking office in 2017, Trump said he would not take home his presidential salary. During his first term, he accepted the payments and donated them to federal agencies. Trump has said he is continuing to forgo the salary during his second term. The White House has not publicly detailed where the payments have gone instead, "In the history of our country, there's never been a president that waived his salary. I'm the only schmuck. I get no credit for it," he said at an event in Rome, Georgia, in February. The New York Times reported that John F. Kennedy and Herbert Hoover also donated their presidential salary to charity. White House Office personnel benefits Susie Wiles, White House Chief of Staff Bloomberg/Getty Images Another major White House Office staff and operations expense is personnel benefits, such as health insurance, life insurance, and retirement plans. In fiscal 2025, the White House Office recorded about $15 million in civilian employee benefits. OMB estimates about $16 million for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same amount for fiscal 2027. The White House Office also recorded about $1 million in benefits for former personnel in fiscal 2025. Transport of personnel Susie Wiles, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and President Donald Trump in Geneva. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images One of the White House Office's largest non-personnel expenses is employee travel and transportation. In fiscal 2025, the White House Office committed about $3 million for travel and transportation of persons. OMB estimates $4 million for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same amount for fiscal 2027. Tools and outside services A Bloomberg terminal keyboard. credit should read LEON NEAL/AFP via Getty Images Similar to the Residence, White House Office supplies and materials totaled $1 million in fiscal 2025, with similar amounts estimated for fiscal 2026 and proposed for fiscal 2027. Figures for printing and reproduction were also at $1 million. In fiscal 2025, communications, utilities, and miscellaneous charges were $2 million, with $1 million estimated for fiscal 2026 and the same proposed for fiscal 2027. Some of the charges include subscriptions and media services. Federal spending records show obligations of $58,294 for Bloomberg access and $25,000 for a music subscription for fiscal year 2026. Repairs and restoration The ongoing construction of the ballroom in July. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images As a historic building, the White House requires regular maintenance and has undergone several restoration projects over the years. For fiscal 2026, Congress appropriated about $2.5 million for routine White House repairs and restoration, including maintenance, safety and health work, and preventive maintenance. Separate renovation costs have risen significantly. OMB estimates $377 million in reimbursable repair and restoration obligations for fiscal 2026. The budget document does not specify which projects the figure covers, or whether it's related to the White House ballroom project. President Trump announced plans to build a White House ballroom , which was originally estimated to cost about $200 million, though he said it could be between $300 million and $400 million in March. Trump has said multiple times that the ballroom itself would be paid for by him and private donors, which include companies like Apple , Amazon , and Meta, as well as individual donors. Security Security patrols outside the White House in July. Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images White House security is funded through the broader Secret Service budget. Congress appropriated approximately $3.25 billion for the United States Secret Service for fiscal 2026, including about $1.4 billion in protection-specific funding. Those figures cover the agency as a whole, rather than the cost of protecting the White House alone. Security funds aren't just for protecting the president and his immediate family. The agency also protects the vice president, the president-elect and vice president-elect and their immediate families, as well as former presidents, their spouses and their children under 16. The Secret Service said it does not provide "detailed public reporting on its use of funding or personnel for protective missions, and staff move back and forth between protection and criminal investigation activities as duties require." Keeping the White House running is no small feat — and comes at no small cost.

With 132 rooms, 35 bathrooms, and a kitchen capable of serving dinner to as many as 140 guests and hors d'oeuvres to more than 1,000, looking after the residence is a lot of work.

Then there's the cost of White House operations, which includes tens of millions of dollars a year in staff compensation and travel.

Business Insider compiled a list of costs associated with running the White House using data from the Office of Management and Budget and government spending data.

They include a mix of approved funding, money committed to be spent, and full-year estimates. Typically, White House expenses are funded by taxpayers through congressional appropriations. Some costs, such as current renovation work, are listed as reimbursable, meaning that another source will repay the account.

Here's a breakdown of some of the costs of running the White House.

White House Executive Residence personnel
President Donald Trump hosted a Rose Garden Club dinner

Butlers, housekeepers, chefs, doormen, florists, and electricians, among other staff, work to keep the White House running, all under the purview of the White House's chief usher.

About 90 to 100 staff work at the Executive Residence, according to the White House Historical Association.

The Executive Residence reported roughly $9 million in personnel-compensation obligations for fiscal 2025. That included roughly $8 million for permanent full-time staff and $1 million in other employee pay. It also reported about $3 million in employee benefits.

OMB estimates the same compensation and benefit costs for fiscal 2026. For fiscal 2027, it proposes about $11 million in compensation and $4 million in benefits.

Executive Residence supplies

Suzanne Plunkett - Pool via Samir Hussein/WireImage

For fiscal 2025, communications, utilities, and miscellaneous charges were roughly $1 million, and another roughly $1 million in supplies and materials.

The OMB estimates similar amounts for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same figures for fiscal 2027.

White House Office personnel compensation
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt.

Mehmet Eser/Anadolu via Getty Images

A separate account pays for White House Office staff and operations, including advisors and administrative staff who directly support the president. As of July 1, 2026, there were 411 White House staffers, including 365 employees and 46 full- or part-time detailees, according to the annual report to Congress on White House Office Personnel.

Salaries and employee benefits make up most of the White House Office's operating budget.

Some of the highest-paid White House staffers include Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt, and Director of Speechwriting Ross Worthington, who each earn $195,200, according to a recent personnel report. While nothing to sniff at, these government salaries lag behind what professionals often earn in the private sector.

Congress appropriated $78.9 million for White House staff and operations in fiscal 2026, the same amount appropriated for fiscal 2025.

For fiscal 2025, the White House Office recorded about $43 million in compensation for permanent full-time staff. OMB estimates that this will rise to about $51 million for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same amount for fiscal 2027.

The president's compensation
US President Donald Trump at the Oval Office, the main office of the president.

Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

The salary for the president is fixed at $400,000, plus a $50,000 allowance for official expenses.

Before taking office in 2017, Trump said he would not take home his presidential salary. During his first term, he accepted the payments and donated them to federal agencies.

Trump has said he is continuing to forgo the salary during his second term. The White House has not publicly detailed where the payments have gone instead,

"In the history of our country, there's never been a president that waived his salary. I'm the only schmuck. I get no credit for it," he said at an event in Rome, Georgia, in February.

The New York Times reported that John F. Kennedy and Herbert Hoover also donated their presidential salary to charity.

White House Office personnel benefits
Susie Wiles, White House Chief of Staff

Bloomberg/Getty Images

Another major White House Office staff and operations expense is personnel benefits, such as health insurance, life insurance, and retirement plans.

In fiscal 2025, the White House Office recorded about $15 million in civilian employee benefits. OMB estimates about $16 million for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same amount for fiscal 2027.

The White House Office also recorded about $1 million in benefits for former personnel in fiscal 2025.

Transport of personnel
Susie Wiles, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and President Donald Trump in Geneva.

Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

One of the White House Office's largest non-personnel expenses is employee travel and transportation.

In fiscal 2025, the White House Office committed about $3 million for travel and transportation of persons. OMB estimates $4 million for fiscal 2026 and proposes the same amount for fiscal 2027.

Tools and outside services
A Bloomberg terminal keyboard.

credit should read LEON NEAL/AFP via Getty Images

Similar to the Residence, White House Office supplies and materials totaled $1 million in fiscal 2025, with similar amounts estimated for fiscal 2026 and proposed for fiscal 2027.

Figures for printing and reproduction were also at $1 million.

In fiscal 2025, communications, utilities, and miscellaneous charges were $2 million, with $1 million estimated for fiscal 2026 and the same proposed for fiscal 2027.

Some of the charges include subscriptions and media services. Federal spending records show obligations of $58,294 for Bloomberg access and $25,000 for a music subscription for fiscal year 2026.

Repairs and restoration
The ongoing construction of the ballroom in July.

Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images

As a historic building, the White House requires regular maintenance and has undergone several restoration projects over the years.

For fiscal 2026, Congress appropriated about $2.5 million for routine White House repairs and restoration, including maintenance, safety and health work, and preventive maintenance.

Separate renovation costs have risen significantly. OMB estimates $377 million in reimbursable repair and restoration obligations for fiscal 2026. The budget document does not specify which projects the figure covers, or whether it's related to the White House ballroom project.

President Trump announced plans to build a White House ballroom, which was originally estimated to cost about $200 million, though he said it could be between $300 million and $400 million in March.

Trump has said multiple times that the ballroom itself would be paid for by him and private donors, which include companies like Apple, Amazon, and Meta, as well as individual donors.

Security
Security patrols outside the White House in July.

Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images

White House security is funded through the broader Secret Service budget.

Congress appropriated approximately $3.25 billion for the United States Secret Service for fiscal 2026, including about $1.4 billion in protection-specific funding. Those figures cover the agency as a whole, rather than the cost of protecting the White House alone.

Security funds aren't just for protecting the president and his immediate family. The agency also protects the vice president, the president-elect and vice president-elect and their immediate families, as well as former presidents, their spouses and their children under 16.

The Secret Service said it does not provide "detailed public reporting on its use of funding or personnel for protective missions, and staff move back and forth between protection and criminal investigation activities as duties require."

items.title: Sam Altman says he got ‘addicted’ to TikTok, including a Saturday afternoon where he scrolled ‘for like 3 hours’
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, seen here, most likely not using TikTok, said TikTok was so "powerful" he had to delete the app that kept sucking him in. Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said he had to quit TikTok. Altman said he began using the popular app when OpenAI was preparing to launch its own social network. Ultimately, Altman said he got "addicted" and realized he needed to stop scrolling. Even Sam Altman is guilty of getting sucked into TikTok. "I deleted TikTok because it was just too powerful," he said during a recent episode of the "Relentless" podcast. The OpenAI CEO said he forced himself to learn more about TikTok as the AI giant began building (and ultimately abandoned) a TikTok-esque AI-generated video social media app called Sora. "I made myself get addicted to TikTok, because I wanted to just learn," Altman said. Altman said he soon found out why TikTok has become known for its recommendation algorithm, widely regarded as one of the best of its kind. "I really thought it was great," he said. "And then I thought I could control it. I was like, 'Oh, it's actually kind of fun,' but I only use it for 10 minutes to wind down before bed, and I'm totally in control of it. And then it was an hour one night. And then some Saturday afternoon, I was on the couch for like three hours." Altman said he knew his TikTok habit was "bad for me," but he was "really enjoying it in the moment like a drug." He said he was able to rein in his usage before ultimately abandoning the app entirely. "I briefly got it back under control, and I was down to five, 10 minutes a night, whatever, like a little wind down before bed," he said. "Then I was just like, enough." OpenAI similarly quit its social media venture cold turkey, too. In March, OpenAI announced it would scrap the Sora app to focus on its core goals, abandoning the concept after roughly six months. OpenAI announced Sora to great fanfare, and even after some headaches, the app led to a historic partnership with Disney . Still, video generation sucked up too much compute in OpenAI's eyes at a time when its archrival, Anthropic, and other hyperscalers were pushing the generative AI race even further. Altman discussed his TikTok foray in the context of how OpenAI is thinking about its secretive family of AI-powered devices made in consultation with legendary Apple designer Jony Ive , which it has said it will unveil before the end of the year. The OpenAI CEO said in November that he wants the device to cut through the noise of notifications that make using devices like the iPhone, which Ive originally helped design, feel like " walking through Times Square." Last August, OpenAI said the "goal" of services like ChatGPT was not to endlessly suck users in. "Instead of measuring success by time spent or clicks, we care more about whether you leave the product having done what you came for," the company said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: I love visiting the 'Napa of the Midwest.' It's an underrated gem with reasonable prices and fantastic wine.
items.summary: Leland, a charming town near Traverse City, Michigan, has won me over with its wine, small-town vibes, and fairly affordable prices. Amanda Adler The wine-growing region near Traverse City , Michigan, is often called the "Napa of the Midwest." It has stunning lakefront views, a small-town feel, and epic outdoor adventures. Affordable prices and beautiful scenery make this my favorite drinking destination. Napa Valley is renowned for its exquisite wine, stunning scenery, and outdoor activities. But when I'm looking for a wine-fueled getaway, I skip the pricey (and often overcrowded) tasting rooms in Northern California and instead head for Traverse City, Michigan. The charming, small-town gem has striking water views and a burgeoning wine scene that consistently brings home awards from international competitions. Often referred to as the "Napa of the Midwest," this boutique wine-growing region offers so much more than just wine. Here's why it consistently tops my vacation wish list. Its lake views and picturesque wineries offer all the beauty of Napa at a fraction of the cost. Amanda Adler Much like Napa Valley, the area around Traverse City is full of rolling hills dotted with vineyards. Instead of distant mountain views, Michigan offers a different beauty: the blue waters of Lake Michigan . The city is nestled by two wine-growing peninsulas — Old Mission and Leelanau — that jut out into this Great Lake, offering a scenic backdrop for a wine-tasting adventure. What also helps me prefer these sweeping vistas to those in California is the cost. Even during the peak summer season, it's not uncommon to find nice hotel rooms here for under $200 a night. In my experience, a decent room in Napa during the busy season can easily go for double (or triple) that amount. The charming small-town atmosphere offers a laid-back place to stay. The cozy tasting rooms found here tend to feel less stuffy than the ones I've visited in California, too. As a casual wine enthusiast, I appreciate how this informal style offers more welcoming vibes. Beyond wine, Northern Michigan is a haven for family- and dog-friendly breweries and cideries. Dog Friendly Sutton Bay Ciders. Amanda Adler The craft brew scene in Michigan is similarly booming, making this an ideal destination for savoring a taste of hops. Plus, Michigan is the third-largest apple-producing state in the US and the cherry capital of the world, making its fruit ciders a must-try. This variety of drinking experiences means there's always something delicious on tap. One of my favorite spots is Suttons Bay Ciders, which features idyllic leaf-peeping opportunities in autumn, seasonal events designed with kids in mind, and dog-friendly seating areas that make this a place my whole family can enjoy together. Michigan's natural wonders provide underrated outdoor exploration opportunities. Amanda Adler California's national parks are known for their beauty, but "Pure Michigan" offers plenty of outdoor opportunities that often feel overlooked. In addition to the ample boating, swimming, and other lake life options found in Traverse City, the nearby Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore features miles of towering sand dunes that feel worlds away from the flat plains most associated with the Midwest. Whether I'm hiking the dunes, sampling local flavors, enjoying a day out on the water, or setting off in search of striking lighthouses (Michigan has more than 100!), I always enjoy a stress-free and budget-friendly stay in Traverse City. items.title: 6,000 student-loan borrowers hoping for affordable repayment plans need to reapply
items.summary: Some student-loan borrowers have to reapply for an income-driven repayment plan after receiving the wrong payment amount. Getty Images 6,000 student-loan borrowers were told to reapply for an income-driven repayment plan. It follows a glitch that resulted in borrowers receiving an incorrect payment amount. The borrowers who received the email were those who manually updated their family size. You might have to resubmit your student-loan repayment application. The Department of Education confirmed to Business Insider that 6,000 student-loan borrowers received emails from Federal Student Aid to resubmit their income-driven repayment applications. "Due to an error, you received an incorrect monthly payment amount," the email said. In June, the department confirmed to Business Insider that borrowers who shared their federal tax information with Federal Student Aid received incorrect $50 payments . Servicers corrected the payments and notified some affected borrowers that they did not need to submit a new application. The department said that the borrowers who received the email to reapply for a repayment plan were those who manually updated their family size, and that FSA was unable to use the tax information on file to recalculate their payment amounts. "FSA addressed this issue and most of the borrowers impacted were able to see updated monthly payment amounts within days of this coming to our attention," Ellen Keast, the department's press secretary for higher education, said. The email recommended that borrowers apply for the new Repayment Assistance Plan, which became available on July 1 as part of President Donald Trump's student-loan repayment overhaul. The slew of changes to student-loan repayment has sparked frustration among borrowers who have struggled to get accurate information on their payments. In addition to incorrect payment amounts, some borrowers have struggled to reach their servicers to determine their repayment options, hindering their ability to manage their budgets. Robin Binkley, a 38-year-old borrower, said that choosing the right repayment plan "is a decision that could affect my finances for many years, and I cannot understand why borrowers are expected to make these choices without accurate information or meaningful guidance."
