items.title: How AI is shortening drug discovery timelines in China
items.summary: Insilico Medicine has reduced the time needed to produce some drug development candidates to about one year by combining artificial intelligence with laboratory research in China, according to CEO Alex Zhavoronkov. The Hong Kong-listed company’s fastest programme reached candidate nomination in nine months, while its typical timeline is about 13 months, Zhavoronkov said. He said conventional approaches usually take about four-and-a-half years to reach the same stage. The timeline covers early discovery and candidate selection, rather than the full process of bringing a drug to market. Clinical trials, manufacturing, and regulatory review remain separate stages. AI shortens candidate selection Insilico uses generative AI to identify biological targets, design potential drug molecules, and assess which compounds should advance to laboratory testing. The company said its programmes typically reach preclinical-candidate nomination within 12 to 18 months after researchers synthesise and test between 60 and 200 molecules. Its workflow combines AI-generated designs with researcher review and experimental validation. Laboratory experiments remain necessary to confirm the biological activity and drug properties of compounds selected by the models. Insilico said its AI-supported process allows teams to reach candidate nomination after testing a smaller set of synthesised molecules, although it has not provided a direct comparison with equivalent programmes developed without AI. Insilico said it has generated 31 preclinical candidates since 2021. Thirteen programmes have received investigational new drug clearances, allowing them to advance towards human studies, according to the company’s pipeline disclosures. The company conducts AI research in Montreal and Abu Dhabi, while much of its experimental validation and laboratory scale-up work takes place in China. Its Shanghai facility has automated parts of biological sampling and compound screening. Teams outside China develop and evaluate the company’s AI models, while researchers in Shanghai handle biological testing, screening, and scale-up. Zhavoronkov attributed part of the shorter development cycle to China’s research infrastructure, operating costs, and regulatory environment. He said pharmaceutical companies with research laboratories in China can remove about two years from traditional candidate-development timelines. China has expanded beyond manufacturing generic drug ingredients and now plays a larger role in developing new medicines. International drugmakers also work with Chinese laboratories, contract research organisations, clinical-trial centres, and biotechnology companies. A Pfizer executive said clinical development in China could be conducted three times faster and at about half the cost of equivalent work in Europe. Drug candidates typically take five to seven years to reach the Chinese market, compared with at least eight to 10 years in Western markets, according to Reuters . China introduced a 30-working-day review pathway in 2025 for eligible Class I innovative-drug clinical-trial applications. Applications requiring expert consultation or involving complex technical issues can be moved to a 60-working-day review period. “We now compete with Chinese pharmaceutical companies on timelines, and with traditional biotechnology companies in the West on novelty,” Zhavoronkov said. Insilico has entered research and development agreements with pharmaceutical companies including Eli Lilly and Japan’s Takeda. The company and Taiwan-based Bora Pharmaceuticals also announced a proposed strategic alliance that could exceed $2.5 billion if definitive agreements are signed and the collaboration is fully implemented. Although Insilico operates research facilities in China, Zhavoronkov said more than 90% of its revenue comes from Western pharmaceutical companies. He did not disclose how much revenue the company generates in China. Western licensing agreements are more lucrative for Insilico because China’s national insurance system offers lower reimbursement rates for highly novel drugs, Zhavoronkov said. The company also limits sales of most of its software within China because of geopolitical concerns, Zhavoronkov said. It plans to expand its research operations in Shanghai. Rentosertib moves towards Phase III trials Insilico announced and registered a Phase III trial of Rentosertib in July 2026. The oral drug is being studied for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that causes progressive scarring of the lungs. The company used AI to identify the drug’s biological target and generate and optimise its molecular structure. The Phase III study is designed to enrol 320 participants across 47 centres in China. It will compare Rentosertib with a placebo over 52 weeks, with the primary endpoint measuring the annual rate of decline in forced vital capacity, a standard measure of lung function. The trial was listed as not yet recruiting when its ClinicalTrials.gov record was updated on July 7. Enrolment was expected to begin in August 2026, with primary completion estimated for October 2029. Rentosertib previously completed a smaller Phase IIa study. The Phase III trial will test the treatment in a larger patient group over a longer period. Candidate nomination remains an early development milestone. Drugs must still complete preclinical testing, human trials, manufacturing validation, and regulatory review before they can be approved for sale. Insilico Medicine has reduced the time needed to produce some drug development candidates to about one year by combining artificial intelligence with laboratory research in China, according to CEO Alex Zhavoronkov.

The Hong Kong-listed company’s fastest programme reached candidate nomination in nine months, while its typical timeline is about 13 months, Zhavoronkov said. He said conventional approaches usually take about four-and-a-half years to reach the same stage.

The timeline covers early discovery and candidate selection, rather than the full process of bringing a drug to market. Clinical trials, manufacturing, and regulatory review remain separate stages.

AI shortens candidate selection

Insilico uses generative AI to identify biological targets, design potential drug molecules, and assess which compounds should advance to laboratory testing.

The company said its programmes typically reach preclinical-candidate nomination within 12 to 18 months after researchers synthesise and test between 60 and 200 molecules. Its workflow combines AI-generated designs with researcher review and experimental validation.

Laboratory experiments remain necessary to confirm the biological activity and drug properties of compounds selected by the models. Insilico said its AI-supported process allows teams to reach candidate nomination after testing a smaller set of synthesised molecules, although it has not provided a direct comparison with equivalent programmes developed without AI.

Insilico said it has generated 31 preclinical candidates since 2021. Thirteen programmes have received investigational new drug clearances, allowing them to advance towards human studies, according to the company’s pipeline disclosures.

The company conducts AI research in Montreal and Abu Dhabi, while much of its experimental validation and laboratory scale-up work takes place in China. Its Shanghai facility has automated parts of biological sampling and compound screening.

Teams outside China develop and evaluate the company’s AI models, while researchers in Shanghai handle biological testing, screening, and scale-up.

Zhavoronkov attributed part of the shorter development cycle to China’s research infrastructure, operating costs, and regulatory environment. He said pharmaceutical companies with research laboratories in China can remove about two years from traditional candidate-development timelines.

China has expanded beyond manufacturing generic drug ingredients and now plays a larger role in developing new medicines. International drugmakers also work with Chinese laboratories, contract research organisations, clinical-trial centres, and biotechnology companies.

A Pfizer executive said clinical development in China could be conducted three times faster and at about half the cost of equivalent work in Europe. Drug candidates typically take five to seven years to reach the Chinese market, compared with at least eight to 10 years in Western markets, according to Reuters.

China introduced a 30-working-day review pathway in 2025 for eligible Class I innovative-drug clinical-trial applications. Applications requiring expert consultation or involving complex technical issues can be moved to a 60-working-day review period.

“We now compete with Chinese pharmaceutical companies on timelines, and with traditional biotechnology companies in the West on novelty,” Zhavoronkov said.

Insilico has entered research and development agreements with pharmaceutical companies including Eli Lilly and Japan’s Takeda.

The company and Taiwan-based Bora Pharmaceuticals also announced a proposed strategic alliance that could exceed $2.5 billion if definitive agreements are signed and the collaboration is fully implemented.

Although Insilico operates research facilities in China, Zhavoronkov said more than 90% of its revenue comes from Western pharmaceutical companies. He did not disclose how much revenue the company generates in China.

Western licensing agreements are more lucrative for Insilico because China’s national insurance system offers lower reimbursement rates for highly novel drugs, Zhavoronkov said.

The company also limits sales of most of its software within China because of geopolitical concerns, Zhavoronkov said. It plans to expand its research operations in Shanghai.

Rentosertib moves towards Phase III trials

Insilico announced and registered a Phase III trial of Rentosertib in July 2026. The oral drug is being studied for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a disease that causes progressive scarring of the lungs.

The company used AI to identify the drug’s biological target and generate and optimise its molecular structure.

The Phase III study is designed to enrol 320 participants across 47 centres in China. It will compare Rentosertib with a placebo over 52 weeks, with the primary endpoint measuring the annual rate of decline in forced vital capacity, a standard measure of lung function.

The trial was listed as not yet recruiting when its ClinicalTrials.gov record was updated on July 7. Enrolment was expected to begin in August 2026, with primary completion estimated for October 2029.

Rentosertib previously completed a smaller Phase IIa study. The Phase III trial will test the treatment in a larger patient group over a longer period.

Candidate nomination remains an early development milestone. Drugs must still complete preclinical testing, human trials, manufacturing validation, and regulatory review before they can be approved for sale.

Industry data have not established whether AI-designed drugs are more likely to succeed in later-stage trials.

A 2024 analysis of AI-native biotechnology pipelines reported Phase I success rates of between 80% and 90%. The same study found a Phase II success rate of about 40%, broadly in line with the historical industry comparison used by the researchers.

The researchers said the number of Phase II programmes was too small to determine whether AI improves later-stage clinical success. The analysis was based on publicly reported pipelines and did not compare otherwise identical AI-supported and conventional drug programmes.

Insilico said it has produced 31 preclinical candidates and secured 13 investigational new drug clearances. Rentosertib is its first programme to reach the Phase III stage, while none of the company’s experimental medicines has received commercial approval.

Automation changes biotech roles

AI and laboratory robotics are also changing staffing requirements within Insilico.

Zhavoronkov estimated that the company could automate or displace about 40% of its software-side workforce. He did not describe the figure as an announced staff reduction or apply it to the biotechnology industry as a whole.

Insilico employs about 400 people. Laboratory scientists and software engineers are being retrained to manage AI evaluation systems, automated equipment, and robotics, Zhavoronkov said.

The retraining is focused on AI benchmarks and robotic systems as the company automates more research and software functions, he said.

items.title: Samsung One UI Hides Notification Categories by Default, but the Setting Can Be Re-Enabled
items.summary: Samsung has disabled the Notification Categories feature by default beginning with One UI 6.1, making per-app alert controls harder to access in current builds, according to Android Police. This feature allows users to block or allow specific types of notifications within an app. It is still available in One UI 8.5 on current Galaxy devices, but must be found via search and enabled manually. The feature is Samsung's equivalent to the Notification Channels system on Pixel and stock Android. Notification Categories: Functionality and Accessibility Challenges Notification Categories allows users to filter specific alert types within an app, rather than enabling or disabling all notifications. For example, Android Police notes users can keep forecast updates and breaking news from Samsung News and Google, while blocking sports scores or Gemini Live prompts. The feature also works with third-party apps. Android Police explains it can be used to allow direct messages and essential alerts from apps like TikTok or Instagram, while blocking spam and video recommendations. Notification Categories is distinct from the newer Notification Highlights tool, as it is an older, separate utility for managing alerts. Samsung disabled Notification Categories by default starting with One UI 6.1, and the setting is now located under several submenu layers. Android Police reports that finding it requires using the AI-powered search in the Settings app, which returns two results: an integrated toggle within Galaxy Themes and a separate "Manage notification categories for each app" option. The correct setting is found in Advanced Settings with other notification toggles. Android Police notes the setting is easy to access only if users know the exact search terms; otherwise, it is difficult to locate. How to Enable Notification Categories, And What to Watch For To turn on How to Enable Notification Categories and Key Considerations in recent One UI: Open the Settings app. Search for "notification categories," and select "Manage notification categories for each app" instead of the Galaxy Themes option. Enable the feature in Advanced Settings under notification toggles. Configure each app individually, as the feature requires per-app setup rather than a centralized page. Access an app's categories directly from the notification panel when an alert appears. Android Police notes this is faster than navigating through the app list in Settings. On Pixel and stock Android devices, the equivalent feature is Notification organizer, accessible through Settings, then Notifications, then App notifications, then Notification organizer. The main drawback is that each app's notification toggles must be configured individually, which Android Police describes as time-consuming. Samsung does not offer cross-device syncing for notification preferences, so this process must be repeated on each Galaxy phone or tablet. Android Police notes that using Notification Categories with Notification Highlights, which uses AI to summarize and prioritize notifications, reduces the number of apps requiring manual configuration. However, full AI filtering through Notification Highlights is available only on recent flagship models, so older and mid-range Galaxy devices do not have this option. Samsung has not announced plans to re-enable Notification Categories by default in future One UI builds or to add cross-device syncing for notification preferences. Users setting up multiple Galaxy devices should expect to repeat the per-app configuration on each device until Samsung changes this behavior. The feature remains available in current One UI versions, so users can continue to enable it manually after each device setup. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Samsung One UI Hides Notification Categories by Default, but the Setting Can Be Re-Enabled appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: Big Tech's next round of layoffs could start with volunteers
items.summary: Some Google employees are rallying for voluntary buyouts to be offered before layoffs. Noah Berger/Associated Press Some Google workers are pushing for voluntary buyouts as a standard first step to trimming head count. Meanwhile, Microsoft recently offered retirement packages on a broad scale for the first time. Buyouts can soften job cuts, though when made available to workers of all tenures, firms risk losing top talent. Voluntary buyouts are having a moment in Big Tech. Workers at Google recently pressed the search giant to make the exit offers a standard first step whenever it plans job cuts — and to extend them to all members of affected teams, regardless of tenure. Microsoft, meanwhile, launched its first broad voluntary retirement program this past spring, offering packages to thousands of longtime US employees. It said that more than 30% of those eligible accepted. The developments are raising broader questions in tech, where many once-scrappy startups are now sprawling corporations — and where repeated rounds of layoffs have eliminated scores of jobs in recent years. Now that many of those businesses have workforces that include employees with decades of service, are buyouts — long part of the workforce-reduction playbook at legacy companies from Boeing to General Motors — a fairer, less painful way to reduce head count than layoffs? And should they remain reserved for veteran employees, as they traditionally have been, or be offered more widely? "Buyouts are becoming increasingly compelling for older Silicon Valley companies," said Laszlo Bock, a former Google head of human resources who now advises CEOs. "They have more eligible people, and it's a softer message for morale." A 'more humane' approach Nearly 100 Google employees rallied this month outside the company's Mountain View headquarters, arguing that the company's past use of selective exit offers should become a broader and more consistent policy. As part of the event, the union presented a petition signed by more than 4,500 Googlers calling for improved layoff protections. Voluntary buyouts "provide agency to workers," said Emma Jackson, a Google employee of more than 20 years and a leader of the Alphabet Workers Union. Alphabet is Google's parent company. Jackson said workers nearing retirement might have accepted buyouts in earlier rounds of layoffs at Google, reducing the number of cuts needed. She called the approach "more humane." Google didn't respond to requests for comment from Business Insider. The company said in a Wednesday securities filing that its workforce grew by nearly 12,000 employees over the past year, reaching about 199,000 at the end of June. Microsoft announced its retirement program in April, making it available to employees whose age plus their years of service totaled at least 70. The company then cut about 4,800 jobs earlier this month. Those who accepted Microsoft's retirement offer received a payout based on seniority and tenure, plus up to five years of health insurance coverage. Still, the formula meant some employees became eligible well before a conventional retirement age, forcing them to weigh whether to leave careers they had not expected to end anytime soon. At 47, retirement wasn't on Marisela Cerda's radar. Yet Cerda, a principal customer experience manager at Microsoft who joined the company after college in 2001, was among those who received an exit offer. Although she ultimately decided to stay, Cerda previously told Business Insider that she stuck around as long as she has because of the opportunity to keep learning about emerging technologies and the relationships she's built with colleagues over the years. The offer prompted Cerda to think more urgently about the next phase of her career. "You move toward what you want more of, versus moving away from things you don't want," she said. A Microsoft spokesperson declined to comment further. Why the calculus may be changing As Silicon Valley companies grow older alongside their workforces, buyouts may grow more attractive, said Josh Bersin, an HR analyst and consultant. Forcing veteran employees to leave through layoffs "creates a lot of bad blood," he said. Peter Rahbar, a New York employment attorney and cohost of the "Across the Bar" podcast, said buyouts might not reduce staff as quickly as layoffs, but they don't carry the same "huge" morale costs for those who remain — or for potential future hires. "How you treat people on the way out is certainly something people look at on the way in," he said. There are downsides for employers, however. Offering buyouts can make labor reductions less predictable, said Jay Zagorsky, a professor at Boston University's Questrom School of Business. If too few employees accept, a company may still need to make cuts to reach its target. "With a layoff, there's certainty," he said. Extending buyout offers to everyone, including those who've logged only a few work anniversaries, also carries drawbacks. "People whom you would prefer to stay might leave," and they could go to a competitor, said Bock, the former Google executive. The risk is especially concerning for companies with what he calls "spiky talent," where a small number of employees create disproportionate value. "That's characteristic of Silicon Valley companies," he said. For workers who receive a buyout offer, Rahbar, the employment attorney, said they should understand how accepting it would affect their retirement benefits, stock awards, deferred compensation, and healthcare coverage. Depending on a company's plans, employees who retire may continue vesting in certain benefits or retain those they have already earned, he said. Buyout packages also tend to be more generous than the severance offers, Rahbar added, and there's an emotional difference between choosing to leave and being told to go. "People are feeling good about leaving on their own terms," he said. "With a layoff, they're clearly not." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The habit that helped PwC's US CEO climb from intern to the C-Suite
items.summary: Paul Griggs started as an intern at PwC and is now a senior partner and US CEO. PwC PwC's senior partner and US CEO started as an intern at the Big Four firm 30 years ago. Paul Griggs emphasizes curiosity and persistence as key drivers for career advancement. He suggests saying "yes" and putting in the extra hours to get ahead. AI is changing how we work, but it hasn't changed timeless career truths — like the fact that putting in extra effort will get you ahead. That's according to PwC's US CEO, Paul Griggs. The senior partner, who started as an intern at the Big Four consulting firm about 30 years ago and has led its US business for the past two years, said he'd give early-career workers the same advice today that he would have decades ago. Success in professional services, and at many of PwC's clients, still comes down to what he called "that old adage that we can't stand to hear from our parents." "What you put into it is what you get out of it," Griggs said. He said the Benjamin Franklin quote, "Energy and persistence conquer all things," encapsulates the qualities required to climb the ladder, and that he had. To him, that means saying "yes" whenever an opportunity arises. "It's putting the time when people are not looking," Griggs said. "It's being curious." Griggs said he worked with an early partner who drew a line down the middle of his notebooks. On one side, he kept meeting notes. On the other side, he wrote questions about topics he wanted to research and learn more about. That's the same mindset Griggs encourages in PwC's newest associates. He said he tells them that, "we don't all get to the same place from the same place," and that diversity is a source of talent and value. However, once they're in the role, they face the same choice: They can leave work on Friday, enjoy the weekend, and return on Monday. Or they can spend a little time doing research on the weekends to better understand a problem, so that they come better prepared on Monday. That person does the extra work because they were curious, not because they were asked to do it, the senior partner and US CEO said. "Monday, they both come back in, and you know what happens," Griggs said. "The person who did the research picks things up just a little bit quicker. What happens then? That person gets more work to do," Griggs said. Eventually, that person gets ahead and climbs into the next role, Griggs said. It may be a horizontal move at first, but at some point, they start to move up the ladder vertically. "Whether it's inside our firm or inside the clients that I've spent the most time with over the years, it is tried and true: Energy and persistence conquer all things," Griggs said. Griggs echoes the same advice other C-suite executives have shared with Business Insider. Visa group president Oliver Jenkyn previously said he blocks off four hours a week to learn something new, and said he only hires curious candidates. Chipotle's COO Jason Kidd urged early-career candidates to "say yes" and volunteer for the less exciting jobs when they join the workforce. That mindset may be more valued by employers than ever. Julia Dhar, BCG's North America leader of people and organization practice , said as roles change and employers figure out how to implement the technology, high-agency employees who actively seek clarity about their roles and build new skills may be better positioned to keep up. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Anthropic Releases Claude Opus 5 at Half the Token Price of Claude Fable 5
items.summary: Anthropic has launched Claude Opus 5 , offering token pricing at half the rate of Claude Fable 5 and claiming near-frontier performance, according to Anthropic and The Register. Opus 5 is priced at $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, compared to $10 and $50 for Fable 5. Anthropic states the model "comes close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price." Opus 5 does not require data retention. items.title: Rockstar Confirms GTA 6 PS5 Download Codes in Japan Expire 170 Days After Launch
items.summary: Rockstar has confirmed that physical PS5 copies of Grand Theft Auto 6 sold in Japan include download codes that expire 170 days after the November 19, 2026 launch, according to a Rockstar support page cited by TechSpot. This expiration applies only to the PS5 version in Japan and does not affect buyers in other regions. Rockstar also stated that Xbox codes are not region-locked and do not expire, but did not clarify why this policy differs between platforms. GTA 6 will be released as a digital-only title. Physical retail boxes will include a download code instead of a game disc. Rockstar Confirms Japan’s GTA 6 Code Expiration Rockstar attributed the Japan-specific expiration to "regulatory restrictions" in the country, stating that download codes work differently depending on the platform and country of purchase. The company recommended that buyers purchase from local retailers to avoid potential activ The expiration period is 170 days from the November 19, 2026 launch. Rockstar confirmed that Xbox download codes are not region-locked and do not expire, but did not explain the policy difference between PS5 and Xbox versions. Following the announcement, TechSpot reported that many buyers criticized Rockstar on social media for imposing expiration dates on download codes. Some compared digital purchases to rentals rather than ownership, while others questioned if similar policies would be introduced in other markets. TechSpot noted that some commentators speculated the expiration may apply only to DLC content, which is distributed via a separate code in Japan, rather than the base game. However, this does not explain why the policy affects only the PS5 version. Rockstar has not clarified whether the expiration covers the full game or only the DLC code. How Japan Buyers Can Redeem GTA 6 Codes Buyers in Japan purchasing the physical PS5 edition should take the following steps to ensure access, based on Rockstar’s guidance: Redeem the PS5 download code within 170 days of the November 19, 2026 launch. Do not leave the retail box sealed indefinitely. Purchase from local Japanese retailers, as recommended by Rockstar, to avoid activation issues related to region-specific code handling. Check if a separate DLC code is included, as the expiration may also apply to this code, and redeem it within the same timeframe. Keep the receipt and code documentation until activation is confirmed, in case any issues arise. Buyers outside Japan and all Xbox users are not affected by this expiration policy. GTA 6 will launch on November 19, 2026. The Standard Edition is priced at $79.99 and the Ultimate Edition at $99.99. At launch, the game will be available only on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S, with no confirmation of a future PC version. Preorders are available through the official Rockstar Store, PlayStation Store, and Xbox Store. Rockstar has not clarified whether the 170-day expiration covers the base game or only the separate DLC code in Japan, or why the policy applies to the PS5 version but not the Xbox version. Buyers outside Japan are unaffected, but Rockstar has not stated whether similar platform or region-specific code policies could be introduced in other markets. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. items.title: Facebook Adds Free Video Selfie Verification With a White Check Mark Badge
items.summary: Meta is adding a free verification feature called Facebook Verified that lets users earn a white check mark by uploading a selfie video, according to Meta's announcement and reporting from Lifehacker. The badge is intended to indicate a real person behind an account and will appear on profiles and across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups. Facebook Verified is separate from Meta Verified, the paid subscription that provides a blue check mark. The feature is launching in select markets before a global rollout. Meta says it will store the selfie video for up to 30 days after the one-time verification. Lifehacker raises privacy considerations around providing additional biometric data to Meta. How Facebook Verified Works and Differs From Meta Verified Facebook Verified is available to users aged 18 and older whose accounts are in good standing with Facebook's community standards. Once a user has access, they record a short selfie video, which Facebook compares to existing profile photos on the account using facial recognition. If verification is approved, the white check mark is added to the profile. Verification is not available for Pages or ProMode accounts. At launch, the badge will not appear on Feed posts, though Facebook says it plans to add that placement in the future. The badge will appear across Marketplace, Dating, and Groups from launch. Facebook Verified is distinct from Meta Verified. Meta Verified is a paid subscription that provides a blue check mark on Facebook and Instagram, and confirms a user's identity based on a review of a government-issued ID and, in some cases, a selfie video. Facebook Verified, by contrast, is free and relies on a selfie video compared against existing profile photos rather than a government ID review. The white check mark functions as a trust signal to other users rather than a paid identity confirmation. Privacy Considerations Before You Verify Meta states it will store the selfie video for up to 30 days after verification, which is a one-time process. Lifehacker notes it is not entirely clear how the video is handled during that retention window, and points out that Meta has previously used user data to train its AI systems. Lifehacker advises users to weigh whether the verification badge is worth providing additional biometric data to Meta, and to read the privacy policy before agreeing to the process. Facial recognition data is biometric data, and the selfie video is subject to Meta's retention and data-handling practices during the stated 30-day window. Users considering Facebook Verified should assess the tradeoff before recording a selfie video: Confirm eligibility, since the feature requires an account in good standing, a user aged 18 or older, and availability in the user's market at launch. Read Meta's privacy policy covering the selfie video, focusing on the up to 30-day retention window and how the video may be used during that period. Review existing Meta AI data permissions on the account, since Meta has used user data for AI training in the past. Decide whether the white check mark's value as a trust signal outweighs providing biometric facial recognition data. Verify the badge placement matters for the intended use, since it appears in Marketplace, Dating, and Groups but not yet in Feed posts. Google’s Selfie Verification Lands the Same Week Lifehacker notes that Google launched its own video selfie verification feature this week, though it serves a different purpose. Google's feature is designed to prove identity for account recovery when a user is locked out, and it grants access to the entire Google account. Facebook Verified, by contrast, is a trust signal displayed to other users rather than an account recovery mechanism. Because Google's selfie verification can unlock full account access, Lifehacker notes it carries additional security considerations distinct from Facebook's profile badge. Facebook Verified is rolling out in select markets initially, with a global rollout planned but not dated. Facebook has not confirmed which markets receive the feature first, when Feed post badges will be added, or when the feature will expand to additional account types. Meta has not detailed what happens to the stored selfie video at the end of the 30-day retention period beyond stating that storage lasts up to 30 days. Thank you for being a Ghacks reader. The post Facebook Adds Free Video Selfie Verification With a White Check Mark Badge appeared first on gHacks .

items.title: I help wealthy families get their kids into top colleges. Here are 5 strategies any parents can use.
items.summary: Lindsay Tanne Howe is the founder of LogicPrep, a global college advisory firm. Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe Lindsay Tanne Howe started a college advisory firm as a Harvard freshman. The company advises ultrawealthy families on how to get their kids into top colleges. Her tips for parents to boost their kids' chances of success include encouraging curiosity. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Lindsay Tanne Howe, 37, who is based in Connecticut. She is the founder and CEO of LogicPrep, a global college advisory firm serving ultra-high-net-worth families. Business Insider has verified her educational background. This piece has been edited for length and clarity. A big misconception about college admissions is that getting into a top school comes down to a single magical turning point. In reality, it works like compound interest, where every small decision builds on the last. Admissions success is built more on how your kids spend their average Tuesday than on any one score, grade, or breakthrough moment. Over the past 19 years, I've shared these kinds of insights with ultrawealthy families and their children, but I think any parent can benefit from the advice we give our clients. Have you worked for a billionaire or the ultrawealthy? Business Insider wants to hear your story. Contact this reporter at jzitser@businessinsider.com . I went from Harvard freshman to college admissions advisor I founded LogicPrep in 2007 while I was a freshman at Harvard. I'd successfully navigated the admissions process myself and, with the hubris of a teenager, thought it was my turn to help others. What started as a summer job has become a global college advisory firm serving ultrawealthy families . Our advisors are all former admissions officers who have evaluated thousands of applications, while our essay coaches are professional writers who help students bring their stories to life on the page. In our work, we don't assume a preordained definition of success. We're not Ivy or bust. It's about helping each child become the most self-actualized, deeply engaged version of themselves. Here are five ways the ultrawealthy parents I work with help make that happen. Lindsay Tanne Howe started advising students on college admissions as a summer job while at Harvard. Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe 1. Cr eate habits that build curiosity The children of wealthy parents often travel and overhear conversations about work, giving them natural exposure to experiences that spark questions. For all parents, though, it's important to create the habits and mindsets that cultivate curiosity from an early age. In my family, we do that by listening to podcasts in the car and discussing interesting articles over dinner. We also take our children's interests seriously. If your child expresses an interest, take them to the library, find a relevant book, and follow that thread. 2. All work, not just a 'fancy' internship, is a good opportunity to build skills We see many ultrawealthy families tap into their networks early on to create shadowing opportunities for their children. It's a great way to give kids exposure to different careers. Students, however, shouldn't be discouraged if they don't have access to a "fancy" internship . Colleges take context seriously, and students should not be disadvantaged by a lack of access to higher-level opportunities. All work is good exposure and an opportunity to develop interpersonal skills, resilience, and responsibility. Some of the best college essays I've read have been about caddying on a golf course or waitressing at a restaurant. 3. Plan early One advantage wealthy families have is that they know to seek advice from a qualified advisor early on in the admissions process. But thoughtful, proactive planning, which is a clear advantage in the admissions process, isn't exclusive to those with means. You just have to know when to start. The right time to start planning is the tail end of middle school or early high school. That doesn't mean asking an eighth grader to start SAT prep. It means thinking about the classes they're taking and where those could lead, and encouraging them to try different activities. It can also be as simple as visiting a college campus while you're on a trip to make the college application experience feel more tangible. Lindsay Tanne Howe founded LogicPrep in 2007. Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe 4. Help your kids find their voice Wealthy families tend to acknowledge and reward their children's authentic voices. In my experience, they really see them as emerging young adults with something to say. They invite their children into conversations with adults and ask them not just where they want to go to college, but what kind of life they want to build. That helps instil a belief in their voice. As a parent, you want to help your child become the narrator of their own life. Ask questions like, "What's the best thing that happened this week?" or "What's your intention for the summer?" 5. Finally, focus on building an 'interesting life,' not an 'impressive application' I really push back against the instinct to build an impressive application . I encourage students to build a genuinely interesting life. There's no perfect applicant or magic formula for college admissions. Simply encourage your child to pursue what genuinely interests them. Do they like marine biology? Take them to the aquarium and encourage them to apply for volunteer opportunities or internships there. The goal isn't to create the perfect applicant. It's to encourage your child, take them seriously, and to help them become the most genuine, engaged, deeply authentic version of themselves. Read the original article on Business Insider

1. Create habits that build curiosity

The children of wealthy parents often travel and overhear conversations about work, giving them natural exposure to experiences that spark questions. For all parents, though, it's important to create the habits and mindsets that cultivate curiosity from an early age.

In my family, we do that by listening to podcasts in the car and discussing interesting articles over dinner. We also take our children's interests seriously.

If your child expresses an interest, take them to the library, find a relevant book, and follow that thread.

2. All work, not just a 'fancy' internship, is a good opportunity to build skills

We see many ultrawealthy families tap into their networks early on to create shadowing opportunities for their children. It's a great way to give kids exposure to different careers.

Students, however, shouldn't be discouraged if they don't have access to a "fancy" internship. Colleges take context seriously, and students should not be disadvantaged by a lack of access to higher-level opportunities.

All work is good exposure and an opportunity to develop interpersonal skills, resilience, and responsibility. Some of the best college essays I've read have been about caddying on a golf course or waitressing at a restaurant.

3. Plan early

One advantage wealthy families have is that they know to seek advice from a qualified advisor early on in the admissions process. But thoughtful, proactive planning, which is a clear advantage in the admissions process, isn't exclusive to those with means. You just have to know when to start.

The right time to start planning is the tail end of middle school or early high school. That doesn't mean asking an eighth grader to start SAT prep. It means thinking about the classes they're taking and where those could lead, and encouraging them to try different activities.

It can also be as simple as visiting a college campus while you're on a trip to make the college application experience feel more tangible.

Lindsay Tanne Howe founded LogicPrep in 2007.

Courtesy of Lindsay Tanne Howe

4. Help your kids find their voice

Wealthy families tend to acknowledge and reward their children's authentic voices. In my experience, they really see them as emerging young adults with something to say. They invite their children into conversations with adults and ask them not just where they want to go to college, but what kind of life they want to build. That helps instil a belief in their voice.

As a parent, you want to help your child become the narrator of their own life. Ask questions like, "What's the best thing that happened this week?" or "What's your intention for the summer?"

5. Finally, focus on building an 'interesting life,' not an 'impressive application'

I really push back against the instinct to build an impressive application. I encourage students to build a genuinely interesting life.

There's no perfect applicant or magic formula for college admissions. Simply encourage your child to pursue what genuinely interests them. Do they like marine biology? Take them to the aquarium and encourage them to apply for volunteer opportunities or internships there.

The goal isn't to create the perfect applicant. It's to encourage your child, take them seriously, and to help them become the most genuine, engaged, deeply authentic version of themselves.

items.title: JPMorgan’s AI leadership is getting a reset. These are the key players.
items.summary: JPMorgan's AI leadership has recently been reshuffled. Bloomberg/Getty Images JPMorgan's AI chief announced her retirement earlier this month. Her departure left a void in the bank's AI leadership and reshuffled the top tech ranks. We mapped out who is now leading JPMorgan's AI strategy as it vies to be a tech powerhouse. JPMorgan has some new answers to the multibillion-dollar question of who's in charge of AI at the bank. The firm's AI chief, Teresa Heitsenrether, announced her retirement earlier this month after four decades at the bank, reshuffling the technology leadership. It's more than just job titles shifting around — JPMorgan said it's restructuring its firm-wide chief data and analytics office as it transitions from focusing on AI infrastructure to business initiatives. "With the foundations now in place, and AI delivery shifting more to business and functions, we believe that aligning CDAO with Global Technology will best position us to continue our momentum to deliver for our clients and colleagues," according to a memo seen by Business Insider. JPMorgan also announced in the memo that Gerard Francis, formerly the chief product officer of data and AI, is leaving the firm. In February, the bank's head of AI research, Manuela Veloso, left after eight years. The bank, with its nearly $20 billion technology budget, has been especially bullish on AI. CEO Jamie Dimon said on a recent earnings call that there are already more than 1,000 use cases for AI, and Business Insider previously reported that JPMorgan can track individual engineers' token usage. With Heitsenrether leaving, here's who is directing the bank's AI strategy and rollout as it aims to remain a tech leader on Wall Street. Lori Beer As the global chief information officer, Lori Beer sits at the top of the firm's technology leadership , overseeing all the systems and infrastructure. She's a member of the operating committee and manages the bank's sprawling tech budget and nearly 65,000 technologists. Beer joined JPMorgan in 2014. Scot Baldry Scot Baldry already had a big job as JPMorgan's Chief Technology Officer, and is taking on even more responsibility as the Chief Data and Analytics Officer now that Heitsenrether has announced her retirement. In that role, Baldry will helm the bank's overall AI program and strategy. Baldry joined JPMorgan in London in 2022, after stints at Goldman Sachs, Credit Suisse, and T. Rowe Price, and reports to Beer. According to an internal memo announcing his expanded remit, Baldry will continue working with technology leaders across business lines to make sure the firm's AI strategy remains consistent. The memo said his team will "focus on AI & data strategy and governance, commercialization and value delivery, and external engagement with policymakers, regulators and the broader ecosystem." Manoj Sindhwani As part of the recent shakeup, Manoj Sindhwani, who was already the chief information officer for AI/ML and data platforms, is also taking responsibility for the bank's data and AI product team. He now oversees the employees who design and build firmwide data platforms and execute the broad strategy. Sindhwani has been at JPMorgan since 2024, after nearly a decade at Amazon, and reports to Beer. William Patrick Opet William Patrick Opet oversees all of JPMorgan's information security, technology controls, and risk management, which have become increasingly pressing issues in the age of AI. As part of his job, Opet ensures that the bank's AI systems are secure and appropriately controlled, and that the firm is protected against cyber threats, including those enabled by AI. Opet joined JPMorgan in 2014 after working at Lockheed Martin and has been in his current role since 2021. He reports to Beer. Mark Birkhead As the firmwide chief data officer, Mark Birkhead's role has only become more crucial as AI has gotten more advanced. JPMorgan has more than an exabyte , or one billion gigabytes, of data across the firm, and Birkhead is the man who ensures it's AI-ready for both LLMs and generative AI. Birkhead, who joined JPMorgan in 2020 and now reports to Baldry, said in a recent post on LinkedIn that "data strategy is the competitive differentiator in banking." Arvind Joshi Arvind Joshi manages JPMorgan's almost $20 billion annual technology budget , including its investments in AI. He oversees resource allocation and has recently commented on the importance of managing the ballooning price of AI tokens on LinkedIn. Joshi has been at JPMorgan for more than two decades and reports to Beer. Sumitra Ganesh Sumitra Ganesh took over as the head of AI research at JPMorgan in February, the latest position in her decade-long run at the bank. Veloso, who left in February, started the research team in 2018, and told Business Insider in 2021 that it focuses on big, "what-if" questions. As of April, JPMorgan had the largest AI research team among the 50 banks that the intelligence platform Evident AI tracks. Ganesh's research has primarily focused on multi-agent systems in finance, according to her LinkedIn. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: How to Store Petabytes of Data Without Renting It From the Cloud
items.summary: Store one petabyte on Azure’s hot tier for five years and the bill runs close to $1.2 million, before you’ve moved a single byte back out. Try to retrieve that data and the cloud charges again: AWS bills roughly $90,000 in egress fees to pull a single petabyte off its platform, and Google Cloud Storage charges even more per gigabyte on the way out than AWS does. At ten, fifty, or five hundred petabytes, that arithmetic stops being a line item and starts being a strategic decision. This guide covers the real options for storing petabyte-scale data outside a public cloud provider: what they cost, what they require, and which companies have already proven the model works. Why the Cloud Gets Expensive at Scale, Specifically Cloud storage pricing is built around a simple asymmetry: getting data in is cheap or free, and getting data out is not. AWS charges $0.09 per gigabyte for the first 10 terabytes of egress, Azure charges around $0.087/GB, and Google Cloud Storage charges roughly $0.12/GB. Cloud providers generally charge four to six times more to retrieve data than to store it, which means the sticker price on a pricing calculator rarely reflects what you’ll actually pay once your data starts moving, whether that’s backups, analytics pipelines, disaster recovery, or a full migration. This isn’t a fringe concern. According to Flexera’s State of the Cloud Report, the share of enterprise workloads that organizations have pulled back out of the public cloud rose from 21% in the 2025 report to roughly 23% in the 2026 edition. That’s a steady, incremental shift rather than a stampede, and cloud adoption overall is still growing faster than repatriation is shrinking it. But it confirms the pattern: companies aren’t abandoning the cloud, they’re rebalancing it, keeping unpredictable workloads there while moving steady, predictable storage onto infrastructure they control directly. Option One: Run Your Own Object Storage The most direct replacement for S3 or Azure Blob Storage is software that speaks the same API but runs on hardware you control. Cloudian HyperStore, Scality RING, MinIO, and Caringo Swarm all deliver S3-compatible object storage on ordinary x86 servers, which means applications built around the S3 API don’t need to be rewritten. Scality RING scales to hundreds of petabytes and billions of objects across commodity hardware, and MinIO ships as a binary under 100MB that runs anywhere from an edge server to a full data center. TrueNAS takes a different route, layering file, block, and object storage on ZFS for multi-petabyte deployments that need strong data integrity guarantees. The appeal here is straightforward: you pay once for the hardware and the software license (or nothing, in MinIO’s open-source case), and there’s no per-gigabyte toll on the way out. Durability comes from erasure coding rather than the triple replication cloud providers use internally, which keeps the physical footprint and the power bill lower than you’d expect for petabyte-scale clusters. Option Two: Colocation Instead of Construction Owning the hardware doesn’t mean building a data center. Colocation lets you install your own servers and storage arrays inside a third-party facility that handles power, cooling, physical security, and network connectivity. Your data stays on equipment only your organization controls, which matters for regulated industries where auditors want to see exactly who can physically touch a drive. For steady-state, predictable workloads, on-premises and colocation deliver comparable total costs, and colocation tends to win on flexibility since you’re not committing capital to a building. Cloud, by comparison, runs roughly 60% more over five years for equivalent steady-state capacity once storage, compute, and data movement are all counted. Colocation is the practical middle ground for companies that want to escape cloud storage economics without taking on facilities management. Option Three: Tape for the Data You Rarely Touch Most petabyte-scale data isn’t accessed daily. It’s compliance archives, media libraries, historical logs, and backups that need to exist somewhere durable and cheap, not somewhere fast. This is where LTO tape still wins by a wide margin. LTO-9 cartridges hold 18TB natively and cost around $90 each, which works out to roughly $5 per terabyte in raw media cost. Storing 100TB on Amazon S3 Standard for five years runs well over $130,000; the same 100TB on LTO-9 tape costs a few hundred dollars in cartridges once you own the drive. Tape isn’t a replacement for active storage, retrieval times are measured in minutes, not milliseconds, and it requires drives, libraries, and someone who knows how to manage a tape rotation. But for the cold portion of a petabyte-scale archive, which is usually the majority of it, tape remains the cheapest storage medium that exists. The Companies That Already Did This Dropbox proved the model at genuine scale. Between 2015 and 2016, the company moved 500 petabytes of customer data off AWS and onto its own infrastructure, a project it called Magic Pocket, custom-built storage boxes and all. According to figures in Dropbox’s 2018 IPO filing, the migration saved the company $74.6 million over two years: a $92.5 million drop in third-party data center spending, offset by a $53 million increase in its own infrastructure costs, with an additional $35.1 million saved in 2017. Dropbox still keeps a small fraction of workloads on AWS where it makes sense, which is the pattern worth noting: this was a rebalancing, not an ideological exit. 37signals offers a smaller, more recent case study. After DHH announced the company’s cloud exit in October 2022, 37signals spent roughly $700,000 on Dell hardware, recouped that investment within the year, and brought its annual cloud bill down from a $3.2 million run rate to $1.3 million by 2024. The company now projects total five-year savings north of $10 million, achieved without adding infrastructure staff. Neither company treated this as a one-time migration. Both built the operational capacity to run storage as a permanent function, which is the real commitment this decision requires. Building the Business Case Before committing capital, run the numbers the way these companies did. Audit your access patterns first: separate hot data (accessed constantly), warm data (accessed occasionally), and cold data (accessed rarely), since the right storage tier is different for each. Calculate a genuine five-year total cost of ownership for your current cloud footprint, including egress and retrieval charges, not just the monthly storage line. Choose an S3-compatible software layer if you go the on-premises or colocation route, so existing applications don’t need architectural surgery. And if you operate in a regulated industry, factor in data sovereignty requirements early: the question isn’t only where the data physically sits, but which jurisdiction’s laws govern it and who can be legally compelled to hand it over. Enforcement is real money at this point: independent trackers put cumulative GDPR fines at more than €7.1 billion since the regulation took effect in May 2018, with Ireland’s Data Protection Commission alone accounting for roughly €4.04 billion of that total. None of this argues that the cloud is finished. Most companies still belong there for compute elasticity and workloads that spike unpredictably. But at petabyte scale, storage stops behaving like a rented service and starts behaving like infrastructure, and infrastructure is almost always cheaper to own outright than to lease indefinitely. That same instinct, questioning what you’ve been told to accept by default, is starting to show up beyond infrastructure too. As AI assistants like ChatGPT and Perplexity increasingly answer questions that used to send traffic to a search results page, agencies such as Liplyn now help brands earn a place inside those AI-generated answers rather than leaving that visibility to chance. Dropbox and 37signals didn’t leave the cloud because it was fashionable. They left because someone finally ran the five-year math. Datafloq is part of Liplyn Information Group. items.title: Sam Altman says one of his biggest fears is that a small number of companies will control AI: 'That'd be very, very bad'
items.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Bloomberg/Getty Images Sam Altman says one of his biggest fears is what he calls "AI authoritarianism." That's when AI is controlled by a small number of companies or countries that gatekeep the tech. A debate over AI access erupted last week after the release of Kimi K3, a Chinese open-source model. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says one of his biggest concerns about AI isn't whether it becomes too powerful in and of itself, but that a single company could control that power. "I think the fight of the current moment is: Are we going to head to a world of AI authoritarianism or liberty?" Altman said on the latest episode of the "Relentless" podcast. "Every time that humanity has traded off its liberty for safety, it's been a long-term net loss," Altman said. "We are going to put this in the hands of people. We're going to empower them. We are going to let society express its ideas and use this technology in the way they want." It's a striking argument from the head of OpenAI , one of a small number of companies that control the world's most powerful AI models. OpenAI is also proprietary rather than open-source, meaning it doesn't share its tech. Altman's comments are well-timed. They follow a debate that erupted in Silicon Valley and Washington last week over how much visibility the general public should have into the architecture of frontier models. The recent release of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a powerful Chinese open-source model , sparked calls from some US officials to restrict access to Chinese models — and warnings from investors and startup founders that doing so could weaken global competition. The divide extends beyond model access. US export controls already determine which countries and companies can obtain the most advanced chips and computing capacity, giving Washington significant influence over who can build cutting-edge AI. Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Google, and many other leading tech companies signed a letter urging Washington not to restrict open-source AI. Anthropic, OpenAI's biggest competitor and arguably the leading AI company on the planet right now, was the only major frontier lab that neither signed the letter nor publicly supported its contents. The company is known for taking a more cautious approach — arguing that increasingly capable models require stronger safeguards and tighter controls. Altman, meanwhile, said preventing such power from becoming overly concentrated has long been central to his vision for AI, even as his company continues to keep its own models closed. "For so long now, I have felt focused on this singular goal of abundant intelligence and a belief that incredible human prosperity will come from that, as long as we don't have a weird power concentration and kind of a new authoritarianism," he said. Altman's comments are well-timed. They follow a debate that erupted in Silicon Valley and Washington last week over how much visibility the general public should have into the architecture of frontier models.

The recent release of Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, a powerful Chinese open-source model, sparked calls from some US officials to restrict access to Chinese models — and warnings from investors and startup founders that doing so could weaken global competition.

The divide extends beyond model access. US export controls already determine which countries and companies can obtain the most advanced chips and computing capacity, giving Washington significant influence over who can build cutting-edge AI.

Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, OpenAI, Google, and many other leading tech companies signed a letter urging Washington not to restrict open-source AI.

Anthropic, OpenAI's biggest competitor and arguably the leading AI company on the planet right now, was the only major frontier lab that neither signed the letter nor publicly supported its contents. The company is known for taking a more cautious approach — arguing that increasingly capable models require stronger safeguards and tighter controls.

Altman, meanwhile, said preventing such power from becoming overly concentrated has long been central to his vision for AI, even as his company continues to keep its own models closed.

"For so long now, I have felt focused on this singular goal of abundant intelligence and a belief that incredible human prosperity will come from that, as long as we don't have a weird power concentration and kind of a new authoritarianism," he said.

items.title: America’s AI Investment Boom Is Reshaping the Economy
items.summary: America’s AI Investment Boom Is Reshaping the Economy Artificial intelligence has become one of the defining investment stories in the United States, and the numbers continue to grow. Microsoft, Meta, Amazon and Alphabet are collectively committing hundreds of billions of dollars to AI infrastructure, while demand for advanced chips has turned NVIDIA into one of the world’s most valuable companies. It’s apparent that what started as a race to build smarter AI models is now a driving force behind investment in construction, manufacturing, energy and digital infrastructure, with effects that are spreading throughout the wider economy. AI Investment Fueling America’s Biggest Infrastructure Push in Years The headlines often focus on new AI models, but rarely focus on the resources required to make those models workable. Every chatbot, image generator and AI assistant relies on vast data centres packed with specialised processors, connected by high-speed fibre networks and powered by enormous amounts of electricity. Building that capacity requires billions of dollars in construction, engineering and equipment, and it creates a level of demand that reaches far beyond the technology sector. These investments are also reshaping expectations for the US economy, with productivity gains and capital spending influencing currency markets before they appear in official data. For investors, forex trading can provide an early view of how global markets are responding to America’s expanding AI economy. Productivity Is Influencing the Next Phase of Growth An important factor to consider is that the long-term value of AI isn’t going to be measured by how many new tools reach the market, but rather by whether businesses become more productive with those tools. That’s a process that’s already underway. For example, manufacturers are using AI to identify faults before products leave the factory, healthcare providers are reducing administrative workloads, and financial institutions are analysing market data in seconds instead of hours. In fact, Goldman Sachs estimates that generative AI could increase global GDP by around 7% over the next decade if adoption continues to accelerate, highlighting why businesses view AI as an investment in future growth rather than simply another software upgrade. Realising those gains, however, will require careful implementation. Businesses must invest in training, establish AI governance, and address data security and regulatory compliance to ensure new tools deliver lasting value rather than short-term efficiency gains. AI adoption is also changing how employees spend their time. Rather than replacing entire roles, many organisations are using AI as supplementary tools that automate repetitive tasks such as drafting reports, analysing large datasets, or handling routine customer enquiries. With repetitive tasks taken off their plates, employees can focus on higher-value work, while businesses can improve efficiency without fundamentally changing how they operate overnight. The Ripple Effect Extends Well Beyond Silicon Valley The companies building AI models are only one part of a much larger ecosystem. This can be seen in how utilities are expanding electricity generation to support new data centres, in how semiconductor manufacturers are increasing domestic production, and in how construction firms are winning contracts to build facilities capable of housing next-generation computing infrastructure. States like Texas, Arizona, and Virginia have become major beneficiaries for companies that want locations with reliable power, skilled workers, and room to expand. Together, these investments support local economies and strengthen AI-powered industries. Financial Markets Are Responding Long Before the Economy Fully Adjusts Markets rarely wait for quarterly GDP figures before reassessing growth prospects, inflation expectations, and interest-rate outlooks. Instead, investors respond to new information as it becomes available, particularly when major AI investment announcements point to stronger productivity or sustained business spending. This also helps explain why movements in the US dollar can sometimes reflect optimism about economic prospects long before those trends are apparent in official statistics (currency markets often react to expectations before they’re confirmed). Investors also watch whether AI investment translates into stronger earnings and sustained capital spending, both of which can influence interest-rate expectations and global capital flows. Understanding the broader impact of AI means looking beyond technology headlines and instead at the elements that influence the market: corporate earnings, employment reports, inflation data, and central bank decisions. Platforms like OANDA support this approach by combining access to the foreign exchange market with real-time market analysis, economic calendars, and research tools that help traders interpret macroeconomic developments. America’s AI Economy Is Still in Its Early Stages Unlike a couple of years ago, AI investment is no longer confined to technology companies or venture capital funding rounds; it’s reshaping supply chains, accelerating infrastructure projects, creating demand for skilled workers, and influencing how investors evaluate the outlook for the U.S. economy. Even though those changes will take years to play out, many of them are already visible today. The next chapter of the AI story will likely be measured not by faster models, but by how effectively businesses convert record levels of investment into increased workplace productivity, and how financial markets respond. items.title: Satya Nadella says trust in US technology will outweigh the allure of cheap Chinese models
items.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella. George Chan/Getty Images Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says trust in America's tech will help keep Chinese competitors at bay. Nadella was asked on CNN about the rise of Chinese models like Moonshot AI's Kimi K3. He said the US's competitive advantage lies in its robust ecosystem of model training, too. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella says trust in US AI technology and its robust training ecosystem will keep it competitive against Chinese products. Nadella was speaking to CNN's Fareed Zakaria on an episode of "GPS on CNN" that aired on Sunday. Zakaria asked Nadella whether Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 — a model that upset US tech stocks — and Chinese technologies have an edge over American products, because they're "much cheaper" and can do what most companies need. Nadella responded that the US has taken an "ecosystem approach" to shore up the competitiveness of its digital sector. "It's been about trust in our technology, right? So, for example, if you take the Chinese models, guess where these models run? They run on a lot of the hyperscalers — that are American — all over the world," Nadella said. He added that because the Chinese models are open weight, US companies can monitor, test, and post-train them. "I think that one of the things that's lost in this is the understanding even of how the US became competitive in the first place," Nadella said. "We became competitive because we took our technology, we built a rich ecosystem where others could participate, in other countries, and trust our stewardship of this ecosystem," he added. "And as long as that remains, we will absolutely be competitive, and we will win." Microsoft has big stakes in the US AI game. The tech giant holds about 27% of OpenAI's for-profit public benefit corporation. American AI companies face fierce competition from Chinese rivals, some of which have released bombshell products that roiled tech stocks. Last year, the emergence of the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek prompted a $1 trillion tech sell-off, one of the first major signs that China could rival US AI capabilities at a much lower cost. In July, Moonshot AI's new AI model, Kimi K3, made waves in the tech sphere for its coding, reasoning, and knowledge work abilities, all of which could rival those of models from Anthropic and OpenAI. items.title: I took a 30% pay cut to move to Spain. I made budgeting mistakes when adjusting to my new salary, but it was worth it.
items.summary: Damien Monel says he made trade-offs to live the life he wanted. Damien Monel Damien Monel took a 30% pay cut at his Amazon job to transfer from Cork to Madrid. He started spending half his paycheck on rent and made some budgeting mistakes, but has no regrets. Monel has more than doubled his salary since moving to Madrid and says following his gut was the key. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Damien Monel, a 28-year-old recruiter based in Madrid. It's been edited for length and clarity. I moved from my home country, France, to Ireland at 19 for a technical support role at Apple, only to burn out in my second year. I was staying at home in bed in the dark, not seeing friends, and I thought, I'm too young to feel this depressed. I knew I wanted to get into recruiting, so I applied for job after job until I landed a multi-month contract role at Amazon, also in Ireland. It was a pay cut and a temporary role, but I told myself I'd take the risk because there was no way I'd keep letting burnout affect me. Two years later, after transitioning into a full-time recruiter role at Amazon, I felt like I'd stopped growing as a person in Ireland. I transferred to Amazon's Madrid office in 2022 without ever having been to Spain, knowing that if I'd moved before, I could do it again. I had a bit of a weird feeling when I discovered my salary would be 30% lower, but four years later, I've more than doubled that lower salary. Along the way, I made mistakes, drained my savings, and spent most of my income on rent, but it was all worth it. Now, I think I'm ready to close my Spanish chapter and move on to what's next. I took two pay cuts without a backup plan Technical support at Apple wasn't my dream job, but I assumed it would be a great way to get started in the corporate world. It turned out not to be the Irish life I hoped to experience. I wanted to work on my English and immerse myself in the culture. I worked alongside a team of French colleagues, receiving angry phone call after angry phone call from unhappy French customers. It felt like I was still in France, and I didn't have many opportunities to improve my English. Moving on to my role at Amazon was a step in the right direction, but I still felt limited. Cork, where I lived, is a very small town, and there was so much more I wanted to see. I started learning Spanish through Duolingo, went on a two-month trip to Latin America, and loved it. The lifestyle seemed amazing, and I wanted to trade Cork's rain for some sun. I asked my manager for a transfer to an Amazon office in Spain, and she offered a move to Madrid or Barcelona . I chose Madrid for its architecture, atmosphere, and overall lifestyle. I didn't care about the 30% pay cut. I had this feeling that I'd taken a risk before and could do it again. I remember crying at the airport before moving from France to Ireland. It was the toughest decision I'd ever made, but it turned out to be the best of my life. My experience figuring it out in Cork gave me the strength to handle more uncertainty. When I first moved to Spain, I spent half my paycheck on rent I watched a lot of YouTube videos about the Spanish lifestyle and got in touch with colleagues living there who could explain the cultural differences and direct me to resources, like a housing website. They also told me about the actual differences in cost of living . I've found groceries to be fairly comparable to Ireland, although some everyday things, such as coffee, wine, and going out for a drink, are noticeably more affordable. I started paying more in rent to live alone in an apartment. I could've shared an apartment to cut costs, but I wanted an upgrade and a place I'd love and feel safe working from home in. I wasn't saving any money, but sometimes you need to make trade-offs to live the quality of life you want. I don't have a plan B. I can't just go to my parents' house if I don't pay my rent because they don't live in the country. I only have myself, and I have to figure it out. I made budgeting mistakes, but I'm happy I did Poor budgeting put me in stupid situations, and I had months where I went completely over budget and was basically living on my credit card. It wasn't the best decision because I paid a lot in interest and brought my savings down to zero, but it was my choice. I'm happy I did because I've had a great experience living alone. I've enjoyed the Spanish life as I wanted to live it. Looking back, I would've appreciated making smarter choices by spending and going out less, but I was young and wanted to get to know people. I messed up, but I'm happy I did. Two years ago, I left Amazon for a higher-paying corporate job and also started a coaching business on the side. Since then, I've been in a much more stable financial situation. I figured it out exactly as I knew I would. Your decisions don't have to make sense to the people around you If I have a gut feeling that something feels right, even if it doesn't make much sense on paper, I try to trust it. People have told me I'm insane for moving or taking a pay cut, but my gut tells me what the right next step is. I'm already planning my next move: I'll be in Dubai by the end of the year. The idea came up during a call with my manager, and I've set my mind on it. We tend to overthink our decisions. A move, for example, is a big decision, but what is the cost of you — emotionally, physically, financially — staying in your current situation? Do you have a story to share about taking a pay cut? If so, please reach out to the reporter at tmartinelli@businessinsider.com. Read the original article on Business Insider

It wasn't the best decision because I paid a lot in interest and brought my savings down to zero, but it was my choice. I'm happy I did because I've had a great experience living alone.

Two years ago, I left Amazon for a higher-paying corporate job and also started a coaching business on the side. Since then, I've been in a much more stable financial situation. I figured it out exactly as I knew I would.

If I have a gut feeling that something feels right, even if it doesn't make much sense on paper, I try to trust it. People have told me I'm insane for moving or taking a pay cut, but my gut tells me what the right next step is.

I'm already planning my next move: I'll be in Dubai by the end of the year. The idea came up during a call with my manager, and I've set my mind on it.

We tend to overthink our decisions. A move, for example, is a big decision, but what is the cost of you — emotionally, physically, financially — staying in your current situation?
