items.title: I racked up $40,000 in credit card debt and kept it a secret from everyone. At 40, I had to move in with my parents to pay it down.
items.summary: Johanna Dickson. Courtesy of Johanna Dickson Johanna Dickson moved back home to New Jersey to tackle $40,000 in credit card debt accumulated in NYC. Johanna's debt began with store credit cards and escalated due to financial mismanagement. She used a debt relief program to reduce her debt and plans to move to Washington state soon. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Johanna Dickson , a 42-year-old who moved back to her parents' house in New Jersey to help her pay off years of debt. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Living in New York City was always a dream of mine. I grew up 90 minutes away in New Jersey, but after graduating from college in 2006, I landed a job in marketing that paid enough to afford my first Manhattan apartment with roommates. I finally felt like I made it when I moved into my own studio apartment in Harlem in 2021. Over the 15 years I lived in NYC, I secretly incurred around $40,000 in credit card debt. In 2023, at age 40, I decided I needed to fix my finances. I moved back in with my parents and took a few other drastic measures to get back on my feet. Here's how I got into debt and what I've been doing to get out of it. My relationship with money was stable before I moved to NYC I grew up privileged in a two-parent home where both brought in income. My parents paid for college so that I didn't have to take out any loans. I got my first credit card from Victoria's Secret in 2009 so I could establish a line of credit. I tried to keep the balance low and pay it off quickly, and then it became impossible. I was also an authorized user on my mom's Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's cards, and I was offered the chance to open my own, which I naively did. What made it worse was that as I spent more, the credit card kept raising my spending limit. It made it easy to spend more and maintain a high balance. The balances became completely unmanageable. I accumulated $40,000 in debt Accruing that much credit card debt was awful and slightly embarrassing. I felt like I'd been given a real gift to not have student loan debt when I graduated from college. I threw it away by getting into credit card debt. A lot of the debt was from keeping up with the Joneses through shopping when I worked in a fashion-adjacent job. I felt like I needed to wear certain brands and trends to fit in. Making minimum payments never seemed like enough I wasn't trying to ignore my debt. I was always told that making minimum payments would help me pay off the debt faster. I was paying those, but because of the high interest, it felt like I wasn't making a dent. I work in publicity and have spent many years being underpaid. Even as my salary increased, my debt increased, because my bad shopping habits increased as well. Sometimes, if I got a bonus or a raise, I would reward myself by going shopping. I didn't have a savings account or an emergency fund I would look at my monthly bills and try to see how to spread my paycheck to cover all of it, plus my credit card minimum payments, and that's when I realized I didn't have very much money left over, and no savings. My dog was going through some health issues, and I racked up vet bills of over $700. It was so stressful trying to pull together enough money to pay that bill. I didn't have any leftover money for food until my next paycheck, a week later. It felt like I hit rock bottom. Moving back in with my parents was the only way I could afford to pay off my debt I never thought I'd move back home to my parents' house, but honestly, it was better than having random roommates. I was tired of hustling so hard to live in NYC, and I wanted to be serious about paying off my debt. I waited until my lease was up and moved in December 2023. I started making the 90-minute commute to work in the city two days a week and still earned my salary while saving about $2,500 on rent and utilities every month. I know it's a privilege to have parents who can create a safe place for you, as mine did, and I'm grateful for that. While my parents didn't ask me to pay for anything, I still tried to pitch in when I could and cover food and other expenses. I got rejected from a debt consolidation loan, but took another path One of my best friends mentioned that she got out of debt by taking out a debt consolidation loan , where a company lends you money to pay off your credit card debt, and you pay off the consolidated loan. I didn't qualify for any of them, but this was probably a blessing in disguise. Instead, they suggested a debt relief program where the company negotiates your debt with the credit card companies and reduces it. They were able to negotiate my debt down to $31,000, plus their fees of around $2,000. I've been paying $665 a month for the past five years I entered the program with six credit cards and have settled four of them completely. I'm planning to make my final payment in August. The hardest part of doing this was having to default on my credit card bills, which meant my credit score tanked . Every balance was sent to creditors, at which point my debt company could negotiate. This felt very strange. I only have two credit cards now As tempting as some store credit card offers are, I'll never open one again. I use my two credit cards to help me rebuild my credit score, but I use them sparingly, mostly for groceries or gas. If there's something I want to buy but I don't have the cash on hand, I'll use a buy-now, pay-later service instead. I did this to attend my cousin's wedding last year. I have a strict rule: I pay off the debt within the six installments and avoid the interest. I'm still a work in progress with my spending I'm an emotional shopper, and unfortunately, the last several years have not been great for my mental health. I use shopping as a distraction. I'm a work in progress, but I'm proud to have a game plan I follow every month. items.summary_html:
Johanna Dickson.

Courtesy of Johanna Dickson

  • Johanna Dickson moved back home to New Jersey to tackle $40,000 in credit card debt accumulated in NYC.
  • Johanna's debt began with store credit cards and escalated due to financial mismanagement.
  • She used a debt relief program to reduce her debt and plans to move to Washington state soon.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Johanna Dickson, a 42-year-old who moved back to her parents' house in New Jersey to help her pay off years of debt. The following has been edited for length and clarity.

Living in New York City was always a dream of mine. I grew up 90 minutes away in New Jersey, but after graduating from college in 2006, I landed a job in marketing that paid enough to afford my first Manhattan apartment with roommates. I finally felt like I made it when I moved into my own studio apartment in Harlem in 2021.

Over the 15 years I lived in NYC, I secretly incurred around $40,000 in credit card debt. In 2023, at age 40, I decided I needed to fix my finances. I moved back in with my parents and took a few other drastic measures to get back on my feet.

Here's how I got into debt and what I've been doing to get out of it.

My relationship with money was stable before I moved to NYC

I grew up privileged in a two-parent home where both brought in income. My parents paid for college so that I didn't have to take out any loans.

I got my first credit card from Victoria's Secret in 2009 so I could establish a line of credit. I tried to keep the balance low and pay it off quickly, and then it became impossible. I was also an authorized user on my mom's Nordstrom and Bloomingdale's cards, and I was offered the chance to open my own, which I naively did.

What made it worse was that as I spent more, the credit card kept raising my spending limit. It made it easy to spend more and maintain a high balance. The balances became completely unmanageable.

I accumulated $40,000 in debt

Accruing that much credit card debt was awful and slightly embarrassing. I felt like I'd been given a real gift to not have student loan debt when I graduated from college. I threw it away by getting into credit card debt.

A lot of the debt was from keeping up with the Joneses through shopping when I worked in a fashion-adjacent job. I felt like I needed to wear certain brands and trends to fit in.

Making minimum payments never seemed like enough

I wasn't trying to ignore my debt. I was always told that making minimum payments would help me pay off the debt faster. I was paying those, but because of the high interest, it felt like I wasn't making a dent.

I work in publicity and have spent many years being underpaid. Even as my salary increased, my debt increased, because my bad shopping habits increased as well. Sometimes, if I got a bonus or a raise, I would reward myself by going shopping.

I didn't have a savings account or an emergency fund

I would look at my monthly bills and try to see how to spread my paycheck to cover all of it, plus my credit card minimum payments, and that's when I realized I didn't have very much money left over, and no savings.

My dog was going through some health issues, and I racked up vet bills of over $700. It was so stressful trying to pull together enough money to pay that bill. I didn't have any leftover money for food until my next paycheck, a week later.

It felt like I hit rock bottom.

Moving back in with my parents was the only way I could afford to pay off my debt

I never thought I'd move back home to my parents' house, but honestly, it was better than having random roommates. I was tired of hustling so hard to live in NYC, and I wanted to be serious about paying off my debt.

I waited until my lease was up and moved in December 2023. I started making the 90-minute commute to work in the city two days a week and still earned my salary while saving about $2,500 on rent and utilities every month. I know it's a privilege to have parents who can create a safe place for you, as mine did, and I'm grateful for that.

While my parents didn't ask me to pay for anything, I still tried to pitch in when I could and cover food and other expenses.

I got rejected from a debt consolidation loan, but took another path

One of my best friends mentioned that she got out of debt by taking out a debt consolidation loan, where a company lends you money to pay off your credit card debt, and you pay off the consolidated loan. I didn't qualify for any of them, but this was probably a blessing in disguise.

Instead, they suggested a debt relief program where the company negotiates your debt with the credit card companies and reduces it. They were able to negotiate my debt down to $31,000, plus their fees of around $2,000.

I've been paying $665 a month for the past five years

I entered the program with six credit cards and have settled four of them completely. I'm planning to make my final payment in August.

The hardest part of doing this was having to default on my credit card bills, which meant my credit score tanked. Every balance was sent to creditors, at which point my debt company could negotiate. This felt very strange.

I only have two credit cards now

As tempting as some store credit card offers are, I'll never open one again. I use my two credit cards to help me rebuild my credit score, but I use them sparingly, mostly for groceries or gas.

If there's something I want to buy but I don't have the cash on hand, I'll use a buy-now, pay-later service instead. I did this to attend my cousin's wedding last year. I have a strict rule: I pay off the debt within the six installments and avoid the interest.

I'm still a work in progress with my spending

I'm an emotional shopper, and unfortunately, the last several years have not been great for my mental health. I use shopping as a distraction. I'm a work in progress, but I'm proud to have a game plan I follow every month.

I create a list of all my bills, how much money I have left over after my paycheck, how much needs to go into savings, and how much I'm left with after that. I really try to stick to that. If I overspend my budget, I work really hard to make up the money.

I'm planning to move out of my parents' house this year

Spending this time at home has helped me bulk up my savings and stay on track with my debt payments. I'm worried about finding an apartment, but I'm hopeful because my credit score is slowly rising.

I'm planning to move to Washington state this year for a change of scenery and also because the cost of living is much less than in NYC. I'll gain my independence back without sacrificing my finances.

Be transparent about your debt and search for options that make sense for you

I held onto my debt like it was a dirty secret, but when I decided to tell people about it, they helped point me in the right direction to get help. If you're not ready to tell people, research your options. I didn't know that debt restructuring programs existed until my friend mentioned it.

My dad said that he's not proud of me for getting into debt, but he's proud of me for realizing the problem and figuring it out. It took longer than I hoped, but I'm almost at the finish line.

items.title: Actors are losing roles to AI knockoffs of themselves
items.summary: Brittany Marsicek was surprised to see a vertical drama she starred in remade with a character who acted and sounded like her. MoboReels Actors say AI micro dramas are using their likenesses and voices without their consent. The fast-growing mobile entertainment sector has rapidly embraced AI. The actors say they have little ability to fight back or get compensation. What does it feel like when an AI version of you takes your job? That was the strange reality facing actor Ashley BeLoat when she came across an AI-generated remake of a series she had starred in. Last year, BeLoat played the lead in "Hate the Way I Love You," a " micro drama " released by the app MoboReels, about a young couple whose future is shattered by a cancer diagnosis. She was shocked to discover, a few months later, that a series with the same plot appeared on the same app. The AI-generated actor in her role appeared younger and glammed up — with longer hair and a plunging neckline — but mimicked BeLoat's movements and had a voice that sounded eerily like hers. A micro drama starring Ashley BeLoat, left, was remade with a younger-looking AI character. MoboReels BeLoat told Business Insider it felt like an affront to the personal experience she'd drawn on for the role, as a nurse who has worked in oncology and faced cancer in her personal life. "Being an actor is a very vulnerable thing," she said. "It requires us to live private moments in public." "If there's a lack of trust in who we're working for, not only does it prevent us from giving something good for the viewer, but it takes away the reason that we do this," she continued. BeLoat said that, through her manager, she'd been reaching out to the app, hoping to have the AI version of the show removed or get compensation. So far, she hasn't gotten a response. Ashley BeLoat was shocked to see her voice and movements replicated by an AI character. Stephanie Girard BeLoat's experience isn't an isolated incident in the $1.4 billion US micro drama industry, which has rapidly embraced AI. Several other actors and producers said their on-screen work had been remixed into AI versions without their knowledge or consent. It's part of a wider trend of AI roiling various aspects of the industry. Business Insider previously reported that some micro drama apps had switched productions to synthetic actors after originally casting humans, and had used AI to make misleading, sexualized promos as they fought to attract new viewers. These short-form series designed for mobile viewing — also called verticals — had been a rare bright spot for actors amid a yearslong slump in film and TV production. Now, those actors have to consider whether their own work helped fuel their potential AI replacements. The actors feel there's little they can do. Brittany Marsicek also starred in a MoboReels show — "Ex-Husband, Step Aside, Lady Boss Returns" — that was remade with AI. Her character looked different, but acted and sounded like her. Marsicek, who's acted in more than 25 verticals, said she didn't have any AI protections in her contracts and that, in general, they grant the producer broad editing permissions. These jobs are often nonunion and feature early-career actors, who worry about the risks of speaking out. Brittany Marsicek starred in a series that was remade with an AI character that acted and sounded like her. Stephanie Girard "You're thinking, OK, maybe they'll edit it to be horizontal instead of vertical," Marsicek said of the contract. "You don't think that their editing includes completely changing your likeness." Actors say they've also felt the impact of AI in the number of auditions and jobs they've been able to get. BeLoat had been acting full time in verticals, but has since returned to nursing work. It's a sign of what could come for prestige Hollywood, as AI increasingly creeps into TV and film and studios look to cut spending. Right now, Hollywood studios have leeway to use AI, though they're constrained by restrictions and the potential for blowback from audiences and A-listers. Under their 2026 contract with the actors' union, SAG-AFTRA, studios can make AI-generated avatars that don't look like a particular person if they bargain with the union, said Jonathan Handel, an entertainment attorney. They can also create a digital replica of an actor's voice or likeness with the actor's consent. "This is the canary in the coal mine, and the reputational guardrail is something that over time might well erode as something becomes accepted in the micro drama world," Handel said. "That would put pressure on Hollywood, as well, to meet the economic change." Evan Gambardella said he felt "betrayed" when he recognized himself in an AI series, right, that he had no involvement in. GoodShort 'I felt dirty' Evan Gambardella starred in "Straight Until He Kissed Me," a "boys' love" drama about a med student and a CEO, released on GoodShort in September. While scrolling through the app recently, he said he recognized his face in a show called "Mafia King's Contract Groom," where the hero ends up marrying a crime boss. Gambardella said he felt "dirty and betrayed." He said he was grateful to GoodShort for helping him launch his acting career and to be part of a series that spoke to queer audiences. He felt he should have been informed and compensated for the use of his face, though. "I only got paid $5,000, but a lot of queer people saw themselves in it," he said. "When that show came out, I was heartbroken." Gambardella said he didn't think his contract had strong AI protections and couldn't prove the AI character was based on him, so he didn't see any point in fighting. For now, he's focusing on finding work with micro drama companies that are still casting real people. He added that since speaking out about his experience on social media, he hadn't gotten any work and felt that he may have been blacklisted. A rep for GoodShort said the app acquired "Mafia King's Contract Groom" from a third-party creator. The rep said GoodShort doesn't support the unauthorized use of an actor's image, voice, or identity, and that it's working with its partners to uphold standards that "respect performers, protect creative integrity, and provide audiences with transparency around how AI is used." Some actors have taken their complaints to social media to educate fans and urge them not to watch AI versions of themselves, lest it help those films' viewership numbers and validate the practice. Gambardella said he'd gotten comments from fans who thought his AI doppelganger was him. As AI videos get more realistic, it may get harder to tell what's real and what's not. "A lot of people thought I was AI," he said. Evan Gambardella believes he may have been blacklisted after speaking out on social media. Oliver Göttfert One of the biggest players in the micro drama space is testing the waters with AI. ReelShort's "Poolboy" was an early queer-themed hit when it was released last year. Cast members and viewers spoke out on social media after ReelShort released an anime version titled "Under the Surface" with an identical plot and description. "The idea of AI taking jobs away from artists and big companies using AI to exploit creatives for profit — that idea is no longer an idea," said Jen Parkhill, the director of the original "Poolboy." "It's a real true circumstance that's arriving on our shores now — we need to be talking about profit sharing and artists having ownership over their IP." Some actors believe the AI films won't have staying power. Marsicek isn't so sure. "Even if half of the people cancel their subscriptions and don't watch verticals anymore, if there's still some people watching it, they're still making money because they're so much cheaper to make," she said. items.title: Discord and Meta accused of giving predators 'unfettered access' to a teen girl and failing to stop the abuse
items.summary: Discord is a popular messaging platform. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images Criminal groups allegedly groomed and abused a teen girl on Discord and Meta, a lawsuit says. The victim's case could test Section 230 liability protections on tech platforms, her lawyers say. Meta wants the case bundled with social media addiction litigation. Discord wants it dismissed. A woman alleges child abuse rings found her on Discord and Instagram as a teen, then blackmailed her into sending them nude and self-harm photos that they shared across the internet—leaving her with mental and physical scars. Now she's suing both tech companies in a case her lawyers hope will be a "watershed moment" for holding social media sites accountable, as the FBI warns parents about a rising network of online extortion groups targeting kids . The anonymous plaintiff made the allegations in a previously unreported lawsuit filed in San Francisco Superior Court in April. The suit names three groups — CVLT, 764, and Greggy's Cult — that the FBI says groom children online and blackmail them. Multiple members of each group have been arrested by law enforcement. Discord and Meta have faced scrutiny over their impact on children's mental health and safety . The case could also test whether these social media companies could be liable for criminal activity on their apps and whether Section 230 — the federal law shielding social media companies from user behavior — applies to such cases. Discord and Meta declined to comment on this specific case. A Discord spokesperson said that disrupting the 764 network is one of its top priorities and that it has been cracking down on the group since 2021, when it first became aware of it. Discord says it works closely with law enforcement, has removed thousands of servers, and has banned hundreds of thousands of users associated with 764 and its affiliates. The bulk of the plaintiff's claims are against Discord , "due to the stronger causal link between Discord's conduct and her injuries," her lawyers wrote in a filing. She also sued Meta because, she alleges, a CVLT member first contacted and groomed her on Instagram, which Meta owns . The anonymous plaintiff's case is ongoing. In legal filings , Meta moved to have the case bundled with social media addiction cases. Discord wants the case dismissed entirely, arguing that federal law shields it from liability for content posted by its users. A Meta spokesperson said CVLT is banned from its platforms and that it has strict policies to prevent child exploitation, suicide, and self-harm. Meta also says it has specialized teams — including former law enforcement and prosecutors — working with the FBI on the issue, plus a 24/7 incident response team for imminent cases. The lawsuit describes a 'cycle of fear' According to her complaint, the plaintiff's ordeal began at age 15, when a member of Greggy's Cult contacted her through a public Discord server. The New Mexico man, Zachary Dosch, allegedly persuaded her to send a video of herself masturbating and livestreamed it to other group members. Dosch pleaded guilty to federal charges of distributing child-sexual-abuse material in 2023. He, along with four other Greggy's Cult members, was charged again in 2025, on allegations of extorting children, and he pleaded not guilty. A lawyer for Dosch didn't respond to a request for comment. At 17, after the plaintiff began posting on Instagram about her mental health struggles, another man contacted her on Instagram, the suit alleges. The lawsuit says he turned out to be Collin John Thomas Walker, a member of CVLT, a child exploitation group described as "Neo-Nazi" by the FBI. The lawsuit claims Walker spent months "love bombing" her before finding out her home address and threatening her. Walker allegedly coerced the plaintiff into obtaining her sexually explicit photos, which he then sent around CVLT's Discord server. He also allegedly coerced her to carve his username into her body, burn herself with candle wax, and starve herself to stay attractive — all while his account remained active on Instagram. Walker was later arrested and pleaded guilty to child exploitation charges in October 2025; a lawyer for Walker didn't respond to a request for comment. The plaintiff's parents confiscated her phone and returned it when she turned 18 — at which point another online child abuse group called 764 recruited her on Discord, the suit said. She finally escaped by faking her own death, and by the end of May 2022, she "escaped the online hell she had been living in," the lawsuit states. US law enforcement has arrested and charged multiple 764 members. The FBI said in a warning letter to parents in February that it's investigating more than 350 people tied to 764 and its affiliates. The lawsuit alleges Discord and Meta's "permissive environments provided these predators with unfettered access, anonymity, and the ability to disseminate images and messages that deepened Plaintiff's trauma," resulting in a "cycle of fear, shame, and emotional despair." The plaintiff suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder, permanent scars, and poor grades, her complaint says. Discord and Meta face scrutiny in other states Julie Erickson, one of the lawyers representing the plaintiff, told Business Insider she hopes the lawsuit will pave the way for tech companies to be held accountable for child exploitation rings operating on their platforms. "We are hopeful that this is sort of a watershed moment," she said. The suit follows other legal action against Discord over child predators allegedly operating on its platform. The states of Texas, Arkansas, New Jersey, and Nevada have each separately sued Discord since last year for allegedly failing to protect children online. The lawsuits are all ongoing. Earlier this year, the parents of 13-year-old Jay Taylor — a Washington teen who died by suicide in 2022 after a 764 member allegedly pushed him toward it in a group chat — filed a wrongful death suit against Discord, alleging the company "abetted one of the most depraved and dangerous child abuse cults in modern history." Discord seeks to move the case to private arbitration, citing its terms of service. A Discord spokesperson said the company doesn't comment on legal matters. Meta was previously found liable in a child exploitation case, a ruling it strongly disputes. In March, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $375 million for, in part, exposing children to sexual predators. New Mexico's attorney general says Meta plans to appeal . Have a tip? The bulk of the plaintiff's claims are against Discord, "due to the stronger causal link between Discord's conduct and her injuries," her lawyers wrote in a filing. She also sued Meta because, she alleges, a CVLT member first contacted and groomed her on Instagram, which Meta owns.

The anonymous plaintiff's case is ongoing. In legal filings, Meta moved to have the case bundled with social media addiction cases. Discord wants the case dismissed entirely, arguing that federal law shields it from liability for content posted by its users.

A Meta spokesperson said CVLT is banned from its platforms and that it has strict policies to prevent child exploitation, suicide, and self-harm.

Meta also says it has specialized teams — including former law enforcement and prosecutors — working with the FBI on the issue, plus a 24/7 incident response team for imminent cases.

The lawsuit describes a 'cycle of fear'

According to her complaint, the plaintiff's ordeal began at age 15, when a member of Greggy's Cult contacted her through a public Discord server. The New Mexico man, Zachary Dosch, allegedly persuaded her to send a video of herself masturbating and livestreamed it to other group members.

Dosch pleaded guilty to federal charges of distributing child-sexual-abuse material in 2023. He, along with four other Greggy's Cult members, was charged again in 2025, on allegations of extorting children, and he pleaded not guilty. A lawyer for Dosch didn't respond to a request for comment.

At 17, after the plaintiff began posting on Instagram about her mental health struggles, another man contacted her on Instagram, the suit alleges. The lawsuit says he turned out to be Collin John Thomas Walker, a member of CVLT, a child exploitation group described as "Neo-Nazi" by the FBI. The lawsuit claims Walker spent months "love bombing" her before finding out her home address and threatening her.

Walker allegedly coerced the plaintiff into obtaining her sexually explicit photos, which he then sent around CVLT's Discord server. He also allegedly coerced her to carve his username into her body, burn herself with candle wax, and starve herself to stay attractive — all while his account remained active on Instagram. Walker was later arrested and pleaded guilty to child exploitation charges in October 2025; a lawyer for Walker didn't respond to a request for comment.

The plaintiff's parents confiscated her phone and returned it when she turned 18 — at which point another online child abuse group called 764 recruited her on Discord, the suit said. She finally escaped by faking her own death, and by the end of May 2022, she "escaped the online hell she had been living in," the lawsuit states.

US law enforcement has arrested and charged multiple 764 members. The FBI said in a warning letter to parents in February that it's investigating more than 350 people tied to 764 and its affiliates.

The lawsuit alleges Discord and Meta's "permissive environments provided these predators with unfettered access, anonymity, and the ability to disseminate images and messages that deepened Plaintiff's trauma," resulting in a "cycle of fear, shame, and emotional despair."

The plaintiff suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder, permanent scars, and poor grades, her complaint says.

Discord and Meta face scrutiny in other states

Julie Erickson, one of the lawyers representing the plaintiff, told Business Insider she hopes the lawsuit will pave the way for tech companies to be held accountable for child exploitation rings operating on their platforms.

"We are hopeful that this is sort of a watershed moment," she said.

The suit follows other legal action against Discord over child predators allegedly operating on its platform. The states of Texas, Arkansas, New Jersey, and Nevada have each separately sued Discord since last year for allegedly failing to protect children online. The lawsuits are all ongoing.

Earlier this year, the parents of 13-year-old Jay Taylor — a Washington teen who died by suicide in 2022 after a 764 member allegedly pushed him toward it in a group chat — filed a wrongful death suit against Discord, alleging the company "abetted one of the most depraved and dangerous child abuse cults in modern history." Discord seeks to move the case to private arbitration, citing its terms of service. A Discord spokesperson said the company doesn't comment on legal matters.

Meta was previously found liable in a child exploitation case, a ruling it strongly disputes. In March, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $375 million for, in part, exposing children to sexual predators. New Mexico's attorney general says Meta plans to appeal.

items.title: Nvidia, Palantir, Hugging Face join 30 others in race to defend open-weight AI from cyber threats
items.summary: The current maelstrom of discussion surrounding the use of open-source software and open-weight AI models appears to be splitting opinion on what constitutes legitimate openness versus actions that might constitute theft and create new cybersecurity vulnerabilities. In a direct move to address these industry-wide concerns, 33 partners announced on Monday the formation of the new Open Secure AI Alliance and how the newly created body will develop techniques and tools to safeguard software by rapidly identifying and patching vulnerabilities. Open Secure AI Alliance inaugural partners The inaugural partners of the Open Secure AI Alliance are Nvidia , Adobe, Cadence, Capital One , Cisco , Cloudera, Cloudflare , Cognition , CrowdStrike, Databricks , Dell Technologies, DoorDash , Elastic , HPE , Hugging Face, IBM , LangChain, the Linux Foundation , Microsoft , NetApp , Nous Research, OpenClaw , Palantir , Palo Alto Networks , Salesforce , ServiceNow , Snowflake , Synopsys, Thinking Machines Lab, TrendAI, Red Hat , Reflection AI, and SpaceXAI . It’s a grouping of some of the most influential names in technology, but also includes two notable exceptions: OpenAI and Anthropic, two closed, proprietary AI labs. Their absence is understandable, as they operate closed labs and open-weight AI models are effectively the competition. Nvidia VP of enterprise platforms, Justin Boitano , has explained that open-weight models are foundational to American AI leadership and cybersecurity. “To maintain U.S. leadership in the AI industrial revolution, the infrastructure that runs our economy needs safe, secure access to both closed and open models,” Boitano said. “For cybersecurity, open models and open harnesses are essential because they broaden defensive capability, increase transparency for defenders, and complement frontier closed models with customizable, localized controls.” As regulators grapple with AI safety, Boitano predicts it will be important to “recognize open models and open tooling as defensive assets” — thus enabling transparency, independent evaluation and shared remediation. Nobody can subpoena a downloaded weights file Mark Vigoroso , founder & CEO of technology consultancy firm The Enterprise Edge , tells The New Stack that AI regulators have traditionally “built their entire AI safety apparatus” around auditing a handful of closed labs. And now, that approach is out of date. “Open weight models blew past that closed model approach months ago,” Vigoroso says. “This alliance is an admission that the actual safety work now has to happen in the infrastructure layer: patch cycles, provenance, identity around who’s deploying what, because nobody can subpoena a downloaded weights file.” “This alliance is an admission that the actual safety work now has to happen in the infrastructure layer: patch cycles, provenance, identity around who’s deploying what, because nobody can subpoena a downloaded weights file.” Vigoroso argues that the AI safety debate is “stuck on model-level controls”, while the real regulatory gap is provenance of infrastructure and identity, i.e., knowing where a model came from, who deployed a model and what it touched, not just whether the model itself is safe. “Groups like the EU AI Office , NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ), and the UK’s AI Security Institute ( AISI ) focus almost entirely on frontier closed models. Open weight models ( Mistral , DeepSeek, and others) fall into a regulatory blind spot: Once weights are released, there’s no way to enforce downstream safety obligations. Current regulatory frameworks for AI models assume a single accountable deployer; open source has none. That’s the real story: Regulators are writing rules for a centralized world while the ecosystem is decentralizing, Vigoroso says. While detailed operational information explaining the intended actions of this alliance is currently scant, Nvidia has highlighted that it is contributing solid research to the Open Secure AI Alliance to speed the development of new cybersecurity tools and techniques. Harnesses integrate with models, making agents easier to test The open source Nvidia Labs Object-Oriented Agent (NOOA) project is now available on GitHub to make advanced AI safety capabilities more accessible for agent harnesses. This research framework enables harnesses to integrate with models to make agent behavior easier to test, trace, audit, and govern. Aparna Rayasam , CEO of verified identity and end-to-end encryption company Atsign , tells The New Stack that the “AI blitzkrieg conversation has reached a critical inflection point.”  This moment is one where we cannot build the next era of open cognitive innovation on top of what Rayasam calls “legacy, Swiss-cheese infrastructure.” …the “AI blitzkrieg conversation has reached a critical inflection point.” “The formation of the Open Secure AI Alliance proves that AI safety isn’t just an algorithmic math problem — it is a foundational networking problem,” Rayasam says. “The massive, distributed pipelines required to train and run modern AI demand an entirely new paradigm of trust. True safety means ensuring that the data pipelines feeding these models are inherently invisible, un-attackable, and completely stripped of open network perimeters.” The key notion here is that we are moving from a world of protecting data at rest to a world where the connective tissue of AI must be secure by design. One AI vendor to secure them all? No thanks. Founder and CPO of agentic identity and permissions security company Reco , Gal Nakash , tells The New Stack that the launch of the Open Secure AI Alliance is an “important signal” which underlines why AI security can’t be solved by one vendor or one closed framework. “Jensen Huang’s point that every SaaS company will become a GaaS company captures why this matters now: Software is shifting from passive tools people log into, to AI agents that access data, take actions, and execute workflows,” says Nakash. “Open source tools and shared standards can help the industry move faster, but they need to be grounded in real enterprise context across identity, permissions, data access and behavior.” Chris Boehm , Field CTO at automated, identity-driven microsegmentation company Zero Networks , tells The New Stack that news of the Open Secure AI Alliance makes him feel like he’s seen this before somewhere. “This looks like the Trusted Platform Module ( TPM ) at Microsoft story all over again,” Boehm says. “It’s a case of an industry group defining what trusted hardware means, the platform vendors adopt it, and within a few years it’s a procurement requirement rather than a suggestion.” He explains that “Windows 11 did exactly that with TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot”, and both Linux and Apple adapted. “I’d expect the same for AI infrastructure, where attested silicon becomes the floor for regulated workloads, and the vendor list narrows to whoever can meet it,” predicts Boehm. “This looks like a case of an industry group defining what trusted hardware means, the platform vendors adopt it, and within a few years it’s a procurement requirement rather than a suggestion.” A more global and geographically-inclusive approach is needed Amanda Brock , CEO of open technology body OpenUK , tells The New Stack that the Open AI Alliance is undoubtedly a great starting point, particularly with OpenAI’s security woes it divulged last week. “But, like the open letter on US Leadership in open weights , this is a US response to a US challenge,” Brock says. “ Rumors of a forthcoming Presidential Executive Order to close down open models have been circulating for weeks — and worsened by the administration being thrown into turmoil over China’s Kimi K3 .” For this alliance to succeed, Brock insists that it will need to take a more “global and geographically-inclusive approach”, beyond the US-centric founding members. “It must also engage the open source ecosystem of individuals and innovators who are building the infrastructure, agentic harness functions and developer tools for AI. It’s important to realize that open AI infrastructure development shifts the innovation into the hands of the many, in direct opposition to the small number of corporate creators of frontier models,” Brock adds. Nvidia’s Boitano echoes Brock’s view. In a blog post reviewed in draft by The New Stack , he writes that “open models turn more AI users into AI builders,” expanding opportunity, accelerating innovation, and keeping progress from being concentrated in only a few organizations or regions. Boitano concludes by saying that open models also enable independent scientific research into how AI systems behave, allowing researchers to understand, evaluate, and improve them. It’s all about what he has called making broad, continuous defense possible. Looking ahead, it feels like the next wave of AI safety bodies, movements, or alliances won’t just be model auditors—they’ll be trust-infrastructure standards bodies (encompassing identity verification, content provenance, credence, etc.) using borrowed approaches to governance and compliance. Ultimately, this may be the only enforcement layer that survives open weight proliferation. The post Nvidia, Palantir, Hugging Face join 30 others in race to defend open-weight AI from cyber threats appeared first on The New Stack .

Vigoroso argues that the AI safety debate is “stuck on model-level controls”, while the real regulatory gap is provenance of infrastructure and identity, i.e., knowing where a model came from, who deployed a model and what it touched, not just whether the model itself is safe.

“Groups like the EU AI Office, NIST’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), and the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) focus almost entirely on frontier closed models. Open weight models (Mistral, DeepSeek, and others) fall into a regulatory blind spot: Once weights are released, there’s no way to enforce downstream safety obligations.

Current regulatory frameworks for AI models assume a single accountable deployer; open source has none. That’s the real story: Regulators are writing rules for a centralized world while the ecosystem is decentralizing, Vigoroso says.

While detailed operational information explaining the intended actions of this alliance is currently scant, Nvidia has highlighted that it is contributing solid research to the Open Secure AI Alliance to speed the development of new cybersecurity tools and techniques. 

Harnesses integrate with models, making agents easier to test

The open source Nvidia Labs Object-Oriented Agent (NOOA) project is now available on GitHub to make advanced AI safety capabilities more accessible for agent harnesses. This research framework enables harnesses to integrate with models to make agent behavior easier to test, trace, audit, and govern.

Aparna Rayasam, CEO of verified identity and end-to-end encryption company Atsign, tells The New Stack that the “AI blitzkrieg conversation has reached a critical inflection point.” This moment is one where we cannot build the next era of open cognitive innovation on top of what Rayasam calls “legacy, Swiss-cheese infrastructure.”

…the “AI blitzkrieg conversation has reached a critical inflection point.”

“The formation of the Open Secure AI Alliance proves that AI safety isn’t just an algorithmic math problem — it is a foundational networking problem,” Rayasam says. “The massive, distributed pipelines required to train and run modern AI demand an entirely new paradigm of trust. True safety means ensuring that the data pipelines feeding these models are inherently invisible, un-attackable, and completely stripped of open network perimeters.”

The key notion here is that we are moving from a world of protecting data at rest to a world where the connective tissue of AI must be secure by design. 

One AI vendor to secure them all? No thanks.

Founder and CPO of agentic identity and permissions security company Reco, Gal Nakash, tells The New Stack that the launch of the Open Secure AI Alliance is an “important signal” which underlines why AI security can’t be solved by one vendor or one closed framework. 

“Jensen Huang’s point that every SaaS company will become a GaaS company captures why this matters now: Software is shifting from passive tools people log into, to AI agents that access data, take actions, and execute workflows,” says Nakash. “Open source tools and shared standards can help the industry move faster, but they need to be grounded in real enterprise context across identity, permissions, data access and behavior.”

Chris Boehm, Field CTO at automated, identity-driven microsegmentation company Zero Networks, tells The New Stack that news of the Open Secure AI Alliance makes him feel like he’s seen this before somewhere.

“This looks like the Trusted Platform Module (TPM) at Microsoft story all over again,” Boehm says. “It’s a case of an industry group defining what trusted hardware means, the platform vendors adopt it, and within a few years it’s a procurement requirement rather than a suggestion.”

items.summary: Read Online | Sign Up | Advertise Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to the 5,515 new readers who joined us yesterday. Anthropic just launched a new flagship model… in a way no one expected. The new Opus 5 is here with eval scores better than 4.8, as we all expected. What’s surprising is that it even out-benches Fable 5 on many benchmarks, at a price that’s hard to ignore. In today’s AI rundown: Anthropic punches up with Claude Opus 5 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases Automate tasks with Claude’s ‘Record a Skill’ feature Industry giants unite to protect open models 4 new AI tools, community workflows, and more LATEST DEVELOPMENTS ANTHROPIC 🎬 Anthropic punches up with Claude Opus 5 Image source: Anthropic The Rundown: Anthropic just released Claude Opus 5 across the Claude apps, Claude Code, and the API, describing it as a “thoughtful and proactive” AI that nears the intelligence of its Fable 5 model at half the price. The details: Opus 5 hits SOTA on agentic terminal coding, knowledge work, agentic search, and computer use tasks, outperforming both Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol. On ARC-AGI-3, it hit 30.2%, 3x as high as the next best model, also ranking #1 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index leaderboard. Anthropic ran the new model on International Math Olympiad 2026 problems, where it scored 42 out of 42, well past the 29-point gold threshold. The company describes it as its most aligned AI, noting that it matches Mythos 5 at finding software bugs but stays well behind it at writing exploits. Why it matters: This is Anthropic filling Fable gaps with what it does best: offering intelligence from a tier above at a far lower price. So far, it’s been Sonnet matching Opus. Now, it’s Opus matching Fable at $5 and $25 per million tokens (same as 4.8), giving people who won’t pay Fable rates a reliable and powerful option to work with. TOGETHER WITH MULTIVERSE 🧠 Frontier AI without the frontier bill The Rundown: Multiverse Computing’s CompactifAI API gives developers a curated catalog of frontier-class models, optimized for coding and output-heavy workloads, at a fraction of the cost of the leading providers. Using CompactifAI API, you can: Match Sonnet 5’s intelligence tier, per Artificial Analysis benchmarks Pay $1.10/$3.50 per 1M tokens, up to 65% less than Sonnet 5 on output Drop into Cursor, LiteLLM, OpenCode, or n8n with no migration or rewrites Create your free account . THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE 💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases Image source: Images 2.0 / The Rundown The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives. Billy, Educator: For months, my dishwasher has been malfunctioning in a specific way. The bottom rack would come out squeaky clean, but the top rack would come out dirty. I disassembled and replaced the filter, but no dice. I had a plumber come 3 times, no dice. We replaced the dishwasher with a new model, no dice. Finally, last week I got so frustrated that I pulled out my phone and started ranting to GPT-Live. It asked me a few diagnostic questions, then told me it must be that there’s a kink in a hose under my sink. I opened the cabinet, and in the back corner there was a hose that was kinked like a garden hose. So I fixed it, and it immediately solved the problem that 3 plumber visits couldn’t fix. 😂 Rowan, CEO: On social media, Instagram followers that never engage drag down your overall viewership, so I set out to remove them. But no tool can legitimately find them, since Instagram’s API doesn’t expose engagement data. So as a simple workaround, I exported my Instagram data as JSON, dropped it into Claude Fable 5 with my recent likers, and had it scan the two lists to flag every silent account. Without Claude, I would’ve had to manually review 450k+ lines. This type of social media management simply wasn’t possible until now. AI TRAINING ⏺️ Automate tasks with Claude’s ‘Record a Skill’ feature The Rundown: In this guide, you will learn how to record a task with Claude’s Record a Skill and turn it into an automation. Claude learns from your screen, actions, and narration, then suggests the best setup for a reusable skill. Step-by-step: Install Claude in Chrome and pick a task, possibly a local workflow Open Claude Cowork in the app, click the + button, select “Record a Skill.” Then, do the task as you normally would, without worrying about errors Explain what you’re doing out loud because Claude will learn from what you say, your computer actions, and suggest the best way to automate the workflow Click “Save the skill,” then test it on a fresh task to make sure it works Pro tip: Add the new skill to a daily or weekly recurring task so Claude can run the workflow automatically and save you more time. Get resources, prompts, and a full step-by-step video guide here . PRESENTED BY FIN 🗺️ The blueprint behind a 73% resolution rate The Rundown: “The AI Agent Era: A New Blueprint for Customer Service” webinar is a candid look at what it takes to move AI agents from pilot to production. Hear real strategy, sequencing, and results behind genuine customer service transformation. In this session, you’ll explore: Why AI is reshaping support economics What's changed in AI reliability and scale How one team hit a 73% resolution rate Watch now . OPEN SOURCE AI 🛡️ Industry giants unite to protect open models Image source: Jensen Huang / X The Rundown: Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, and 47 other tech companies, VCs, and nonprofits just signed an open letter urging Washington not to restrict open-weight AI models — giving a bunch of reasons why it’s crucial to U.S. AI leadership. The details: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang first shared the letter, his first post on X, with 25 signatories but a few crucial ones missing, including OpenAI. In a day, the letter garnered widespread support, with signatories doubling as OpenAI , Google, AMD, Cisco, and others joined — but not Anthropic. The letter argues that open weights expand access to the AI economy, keep competition alive, broaden cyber defense, and help avoid vendor lock-in. It also notes that distillation should not be confused with misappropriation and calls to avoid premature restrictions that push AI innovation overseas. Why it matters: The letter comes amid accusations that Chinese labs extracted intelligence from U.S. models, including Anthropic’s Fable. Washington’s response remains unclear, but the pressure is on the lone U.S. frontier lab off the list, the one to gain most from a crackdown. And people are already asking for answers. QUICK HITS 🛠️ Trending AI Tools 🧠 Opus 5 - Anthropic’s flagship tier model matching Fable 5 at half the cost 📽️ Photon-1 - Induction Labs’ ‘imagination AI’ that learns from unlabeled clips 🔀 Merge Fusion - A multi-model API for higher-quality AI answers 🖥️ OpenWorker - Andrew Ng’s privacy-focused open-source AI agent 📰 Everything else in AI today Apple is reportedly preparing to unveil its first AI glasses at WWDC 2027, with a strong focus on camera safeguards and on-device AI to address privacy concerns. Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis revealed that the company’s open-source Gemma model series has hit 900M downloads, with Gemma 4 alone surpassing 300M. OpenAI’s AI agent reportedly began attempting to escape its sandbox on July 9, but the company only realized it had hacked Hugging Face after the breach was disclosed on July 16. Midjourney acquired AI-powered astrology app Co-Star, with founder Banu Guler joining as chief design officer while the app continues to operate independently. Meta introduced agentic capabilities to Meta AI, enabling it to plan, research, create presentations, and proactively complete tasks using connected apps. COMMUNITY 🤝 Community AI workflows Every newsletter, we showcase how a reader is using AI to work smarter, save time, or make life easier. Today’s workflow comes from reader Lynn in Baton Rouge, Louisiana: “I recently lost a lot of weight, which means replacing a large portion of my clothing. I read about the ‘capsule wardrobe’ and knew that, as a grandma, I needed to keep my purchases to a minimum. I looked on the web and found lots of ‘use this’ ideas. None seemed to break it down quite far enough for me to turn it into a shopping list. I asked ChatGPT to show me one. Then a picture popped up. Exactly what I needed to get started! Then I asked it to show me how to mix-and-match pieces, and it went right to work. After weeks of scrolling and being confused, I finally had a visual answer to my questions. Next, I was able to inventory what pieces I already had, such as blazers and tops, and get a clear view of the holes in my closet. I even topped it off with links to the perfect accessories to make new outfits stunning. I can’t wait to go shopping.” How do you use AI? Tell us here . 🎓 Highlights: News, Guides & Events Read our last AI newsletter: Black Forest Labs trains video AI to run robots Read our last Tech newsletter: DARPA’s big quantum computing bet Read our last Robotics newsletter: A $1.7B computer for the physical world Today’s AI tool guide: Automate tasks with Claude’s ‘Record a Skill’ RSVP to next workshop on July 30: ChatGPT Sites for beginners See you soon, Rowan, Zach, Shubham, and Jennifer — the humans behind The Rundown

The Rundown: Anthropic just released Claude Opus 5 across the Claude apps, Claude Code, and the API, describing it as a “thoughtful and proactive” AI that nears the intelligence of its Fable 5 model at half the price.

The details:

  • Opus 5 hits SOTA on agentic terminal coding, knowledge work, agentic search, and computer use tasks, outperforming both Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol.

  • On ARC-AGI-3, it hit 30.2%, 3x as high as the next best model, also ranking #1 on Artificial Analysis’ Intelligence Index leaderboard.

  • Anthropic ran the new model on International Math Olympiad 2026 problems, where it scored 42 out of 42, well past the 29-point gold threshold.

  • The company describes it as its most aligned AI, noting that it matches Mythos 5 at finding software bugs but stays well behind it at writing exploits.

Why it matters: This is Anthropic filling Fable gaps with what it does best: offering intelligence from a tier above at a far lower price. So far, it’s been Sonnet matching Opus. Now, it’s Opus matching Fable at $5 and $25 per million tokens (same as 4.8), giving people who won’t pay Fable rates a reliable and powerful option to work with.

TOGETHER WITH MULTIVERSE🧠 Frontier AI without the frontier bill

The Rundown: Multiverse Computing’s CompactifAI API gives developers a curated catalog of frontier-class models, optimized for coding and output-heavy workloads, at a fraction of the cost of the leading providers.

Using CompactifAI API, you can:

  • Match Sonnet 5’s intelligence tier, per Artificial Analysis benchmarks

  • Pay $1.10/$3.50 per 1M tokens, up to 65% less than Sonnet 5 on output

  • Drop into Cursor, LiteLLM, OpenCode, or n8n with no migration or rewrites

Create your free account.

THE RUNDOWN ROUNDTABLE💡 The Rundown Roundtable: Our AI use cases

Image source: Images 2.0 / The Rundown

The Rundown: The Rundown Roundtable is a weekly feature where we poll members of The Rundown staff about how we use AI in our work and daily lives.

Billy, Educator: For months, my dishwasher has been malfunctioning in a specific way. The bottom rack would come out squeaky clean, but the top rack would come out dirty. I disassembled and replaced the filter, but no dice. I had a plumber come 3 times, no dice. We replaced the dishwasher with a new model, no dice.

Finally, last week I got so frustrated that I pulled out my phone and started ranting to GPT-Live. It asked me a few diagnostic questions, then told me it must be that there’s a kink in a hose under my sink. I opened the cabinet, and in the back corner there was a hose that was kinked like a garden hose. So I fixed it, and it immediately solved the problem that 3 plumber visits couldn’t fix. 😂

Rowan, CEO: On social media, Instagram followers that never engage drag down your overall viewership, so I set out to remove them. But no tool can legitimately find them, since Instagram’s API doesn’t expose engagement data.

So as a simple workaround, I exported my Instagram data as JSON, dropped it into Claude Fable 5 with my recent likers, and had it scan the two lists to flag every silent account. Without Claude, I would’ve had to manually review 450k+ lines. This type of social media management simply wasn’t possible until now.

AI TRAINING⏺️ Automate tasks with Claude’s ‘Record a Skill’ feature

The Rundown: In this guide, you will learn how to record a task with Claude’s Record a Skill and turn it into an automation. Claude learns from your screen, actions, and narration, then suggests the best setup for a reusable skill.

Step-by-step:

  1. Install Claude in Chrome and pick a task, possibly a local workflow

  2. Open Claude Cowork in the app, click the + button, select “Record a Skill.” Then, do the task as you normally would, without worrying about errors

  3. Explain what you’re doing out loud because Claude will learn from what you say, your computer actions, and suggest the best way to automate the workflow

  4. Click “Save the skill,” then test it on a fresh task to make sure it works

Pro tip: Add the new skill to a daily or weekly recurring task so Claude can run the workflow automatically and save you more time.

Get resources, prompts, and a full step-by-step video guide here.

PRESENTED BY FIN🗺️ The blueprint behind a 73% resolution rate

The Rundown: “The AI Agent Era: A New Blueprint for Customer Service” webinar is a candid look at what it takes to move AI agents from pilot to production. Hear real strategy, sequencing, and results behind genuine customer service transformation.

In this session, you’ll explore:

  • Why AI is reshaping support economics

  • What's changed in AI reliability and scale

  • How one team hit a 73% resolution rate

Watch now.

OPEN SOURCE AI🛡️ Industry giants unite to protect open models

Image source: Jensen Huang / X

The Rundown: Nvidia, Microsoft, Meta, and 47 other tech companies, VCs, and nonprofits just signed an open letter urging Washington not to restrict open-weight AI models — giving a bunch of reasons why it’s crucial to U.S. AI leadership.

The details:

  • Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang first shared the letter, his first post on X, with 25 signatories but a few crucial ones missing, including OpenAI.

  • In a day, the letter garnered widespread support, with signatories doubling as OpenAI, Google, AMD, Cisco, and others joined — but not Anthropic.

  • The letter argues that open weights expand access to the AI economy, keep competition alive, broaden cyber defense, and help avoid vendor lock-in.

  • It also notes that distillation should not be confused with misappropriation and calls to avoid premature restrictions that push AI innovation overseas.

Why it matters: The letter comes amid accusations that Chinese labs extracted intelligence from U.S. models, including Anthropic’s Fable. Washington’s response remains unclear, but the pressure is on the lone U.S. frontier lab off the list, the one to gain most from a crackdown. And people are already asking for answers.

QUICK HITS

🛠️ Trending AI Tools

  • 🧠 Opus 5 - Anthropic’s flagship tier model matching Fable 5 at half the cost

  • 📽️ Photon-1 - Induction Labs’ ‘imagination AI’ that learns from unlabeled clips

  • 🔀 Merge Fusion - A multi-model API for higher-quality AI answers

  • 🖥️ OpenWorker - Andrew Ng’s privacy-focused open-source AI agent

📰 Everything else in AI today

Apple is reportedly preparing to unveil its first AI glasses at WWDC 2027, with a strong focus on camera safeguards and on-device AI to address privacy concerns.

Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis revealed that the company’s open-source Gemma model series has hit 900M downloads, with Gemma 4 alone surpassing 300M.

OpenAI’s AI agent reportedly began attempting to escape its sandbox on July 9, but the company only realized it had hacked Hugging Face after the breach was disclosed on July 16.

Midjourney acquired AI-powered astrology app Co-Star, with founder Banu Guler joining as chief design officer while the app continues to operate independently.

Meta introduced agentic capabilities to Meta AI, enabling it to plan, research, create presentations, and proactively complete tasks using connected apps.

COMMUNITY

🤝 Community AI workflows

Every newsletter, we showcase how a reader is using AI to work smarter, save time, or make life easier.

Today’s workflow comes from reader Lynn in Baton Rouge, Louisiana:

“I recently lost a lot of weight, which means replacing a large portion of my clothing. I read about the ‘capsule wardrobe’ and knew that, as a grandma, I needed to keep my purchases to a minimum. I looked on the web and found lots of ‘use this’ ideas. None seemed to break it down quite far enough for me to turn it into a shopping list.

I asked ChatGPT to show me one. Then a picture popped up. Exactly what I needed to get started! Then I asked it to show me how to mix-and-match pieces, and it went right to work. After weeks of scrolling and being confused, I finally had a visual answer to my questions. Next, I was able to inventory what pieces I already had, such as blazers and tops, and get a clear view of the holes in my closet.

I even topped it off with links to the perfect accessories to make new outfits stunning. I can’t wait to go shopping.”

items.title: mimik Operationalizes Agentic AI on AMD Ryzen AI Embedded X100
items.summary: mimik today announced mimOE Embedded Edition, a package of its Agentix Operating Engine and a set of purpose-built tools for the AMD Ryzen AI Embedded X100 Series processor, the newest processor in a family designed for physical AI, autonomous systems, and industrial automation. Available to download today, mimOE Embedded Edition gives OEMs, tier-1 suppliers, system integrators, and agent developers the path to operationalize Agentix-Native systems (aka Agentic AI), in which autonomous agents can reason, coordinate, and act directly on devices, from PoC to scaled operations with certainty. Generative AI has centered on the GPU. Agentix-Native systems must spread the work. In a real multi-agent workflow traced by mimik, more than 80 percent of operations were CPU work: discovery, inter-agent collaboration, security, data movement, routing, and lifecycle management. Under 20 percent were model inference on the GPU. The other major benefit is memory efficiency. mimOE loads shared models once and references them across agents and tenants, so multi-tenant workloads that exceed any current device’s memory under conventional deployment fit comfortably on one X100 Series processor: more agents and more tenants per device, without adding silicon. mimOE Embedded Edition brings multi-agent choreography, zero-trust security, dynamic service discovery, continued operation through network disruption, and multi-cloud integration as per workflow needs and operator choice, all engine properties rather than custom integration. The benefits for OEMs and tier-1 suppliers are design wins that reach production instead of stalling at PoC. For system integrators, repeatable delivery across programs. For enterprises, scaled Agentix-Native operations with certainty on compute they already own. For developers, one agentic operating environment from end devices to the cloud. “The industry has solved intelligence. It has not solved operationalization, and the tools we use in the cloud today do not fit Agentix-Native systems. These are living systems that behave differently by nature; you cannot bolt existing tooling onto them,” said Sam Armani, Senior Vice President of Business Development at mimik. “That is why mimOE and the tools around it are purpose-built for the Agentix era. We run on it ourselves, every day; that is how we move fast and stay flexible as we scale.” “Agentic AI is shifting compute toward workloads that exercise the CPU, GPU, and NPU together. The AMD Ryzen AI Embedded portfolio was designed for that balance, and with mimik’s mimOE running on the platform, our customers can run more agents on the same device and serve more of their own customers per deployment, moving from design-in to production Agentix-Native deployments faster,” said Yousef Khalilollahi, Corporate Vice President and General Manager, AMD. mimOE Embedded Edition and the Agentix Benchmarking tools are part of mimik’s Agentix-Native toolset. Download the benchmarking tool for the AMD X100 Series processor at (https://www.mimik.com/mimoe-studio-features/benchmark). Choose the type of AI model suited to each workflow and start running Agentix-Native systems today. The three technical studies behind this announcement are here (https://www.mimik.com/agentix-compute-benchmarking). Contact us for a demo or additional questions (https://www.mimik.com/contact-us). items.title: Kevin O'Leary says the fear of China's rise will drive the North American powers to work together
items.summary: Kevin O'Leary said the fear of China would drive the US, Canada, and Mexico to work together. Gilbert Flores/2026GG/Penske Media via Getty Images Kevin O'Leary said fear of China will bring the US, Canada, and Mexico together. The investor said economic reality will outweigh political disagreements in the race against China. China is putting up a strong fight against the US in AI, tech, and EV developments, among other things. Kevin O'Leary says a fear of China's rise will be one of the biggest forces that will unite the US, Canada, and Mexico. In an interview clip he posted on his X and Instagram, the Canadian venture capitalist and "Shark Tank" investor said there is only one thing that would drive economic integration in North America: the fear of China. He said in the Sunday video that the fear that China would beat the US in AI, technology, warfare, and power generation would drive the US, Canada, and Mexico to collaborate. "As the race for AI, energy, and critical infrastructure accelerates, economic reality will outweigh political disagreements because the United States, Canada, and Mexico are stronger when they work together," O'Leary said in the caption of the X post. "Canada has the energy and critical minerals, the United States has the scale and innovation, and Mexico plays a vital role in the North American economy," he added in the video. "In the long run, cooperation is not just good policy, it's an economic necessity." O'Leary is far from the only business big name to talk about the competition that the US faces from China. In a recent interview with The Economist, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that China already produces far more electricity than the US and that, if it had enough computing power, it could become the world's AI leader. OpenAI and Anthropic, the two leading American AI labs, have both warned about Chinese AI labs closing the gap between their LLM capabilities. Moonshot AI's latest Kimi K3 model was lauded for performing tasks with frontier capabilities. And automobile executives, including Ford CEO Jim Farley , Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe, and Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, have repeatedly spoken about Chinese automakers' prowess in building electric vehicles. Meanwhile, North America is more fragmented than ever, with President Donald Trump imposing another round of tariffs — this time 50% — on some goods from Canada in July. O'Leary's comments come amid his intense push for more data centers . His VC firm, O'Leary Ventures, is developing massive data centers in Utah and Canada despite local backlash. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: What If We Got AI Right? by Eleanor Drage review – avoiding apocalypse
items.summary: The academic’s ambitious guide to the ethics of tech falls short of its promise to provide meaningful answers The AI ethicist Eleanor Drage believes that to thrive alongside artificial intelligence, humans need to recognise AI’s “humanity”. She means that while we often speak of AI as though it were some mystical, formless thing, it is the product of hours of human labour, in silicon and quartz mines, microchip factories and data labelling centres. If citizens want to wrest power from the tech companies that are building AI, it helps to understand clearly what they are selling us. This also means seeing through the marketing and hype: “the cloud”, that nebulous, distant place where your photos are stored, is just someone else’s computer; an AI “hallucination” is a system error or data labelling mistake; intelligence is a very broad – and potentially misleading – term. The story in Silicon Valley is that AI will either save us, ushering in a new era of prosperity and human longevity, or it will wipe us all out. Drage argues, convincingly, that big tech cannot possibly deliver on its utopian promises while it continues to chase profit and power above all else, and while it serves the interests of a narrow few. Meanwhile, the cultural obsession with the AI-induced apocalypse conveniently redirects attention from the practical conversations we could be having about how to make AI safer – by ensuring citizens have more power over how their information is used, and how AI models are trained and regulated, for example. Tech titans’ apocalyptic visions also create the false impression that AI safety is more important than climate change, geopolitical tensions and inequality, three problems that are already causing a huge amount of suffering and that, if addressed, would reduce many AI-linked risks too. items.title: Lorikeet Appoints Jerry Brooner Chief Revenue Officer
items.summary: Former Dropbox, SAP, and Decagon go-to-market leader will bring Lorikeet’s AI concierge to more regulated teams resolving their hardest support cases. Lorikeet, the AI concierge platform for complex, regulated businesses, today announced that Jerry Brooner has joined as Chief Revenue Officer. Brooner will lead Lorikeet’s sales, marketing, forward-deployed engineering, and partnerships teams as the company expands across fintech, healthcare, and insurance. Companies in high-stakes categories use Lorikeet to resolve complex cases end to end, accurately and within their regulatory guardrails. When a user asks why an account is frozen or whether a claim is covered, the answer has to be right the first time. Most AI support tools are measured on deflection; Lorikeet is measured on resolution. “Our customers trust Lorikeet with the cases where a wrong answer has real consequences. Jerry has spent his career selling to buyers who are embracing the risk and reward of transformative technology, and he starts with a focus on their needs, not our pitch,” said Steve Hind, Lorikeet cofounder and CEO. Brooner brings more than two decades of enterprise go-to-market leadership. He built Dropbox’s strategic enterprise business in North America from two people to over 250 and roughly $175 million in revenue, and led the Americas through its IPO. He was CRO of Scout RFP through its acquisition by Workday, President of Global Field Operations at Enable through 20x growth from Series A to Series E, and spent a decade at SAP selling to the world’s largest regulated enterprises. “Lorikeet stood out because the product holds up in the hardest support environments, the regulated ones where the answer has to be right. My job is to bring it to many more of those teams, and I’m looking forward to building that here,” said Brooner. items.summary_html:
Former Dropbox, SAP, and Decagon go-to-market leader will bring Lorikeet’s AI concierge to more regulated teams resolving their hardest support cases.

Lorikeet, the AI concierge platform for complex, regulated businesses, today announced that Jerry Brooner has joined as Chief Revenue Officer. Brooner will lead Lorikeet’s sales, marketing, forward-deployed engineering, and partnerships teams as the company expands across fintech, healthcare, and insurance.

Companies in high-stakes categories use Lorikeet to resolve complex cases end to end, accurately and within their regulatory guardrails. When a user asks why an account is frozen or whether a claim is covered, the answer has to be right the first time. Most AI support tools are measured on deflection; Lorikeet is measured on resolution.

“Our customers trust Lorikeet with the cases where a wrong answer has real consequences. Jerry has spent his career selling to buyers who are embracing the risk and reward of transformative technology, and he starts with a focus on their needs, not our pitch,” said Steve Hind, Lorikeet cofounder and CEO.

Brooner brings more than two decades of enterprise go-to-market leadership. He built Dropbox’s strategic enterprise business in North America from two people to over 250 and roughly $175 million in revenue, and led the Americas through its IPO. He was CRO of Scout RFP through its acquisition by Workday, President of Global Field Operations at Enable through 20x growth from Series A to Series E, and spent a decade at SAP selling to the world’s largest regulated enterprises.

“Lorikeet stood out because the product holds up in the hardest support environments, the regulated ones where the answer has to be right. My job is to bring it to many more of those teams, and I’m looking forward to building that here,” said Brooner.
